## Ohio Pre-Statehood Locality Guide
**Place:** Northwest Territory / Ohio (present-day boundaries)
**Period:** ca. 1790 — pre-statehood (Ohio became a state 1 March 1803)

### Jurisdictional Context
In 1790, what is now Ohio was part of the **Northwest Territory**, organized under the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Every record generated in 1790 was created under territorial authority. FamilySearch's standardized place for 'Ohio' carries a start date of +1803 — for pre-statehood research, the governing jurisdiction is the Northwest Territory.

**County formation timeline:** All of present-day Ohio in 1790 fell under one of two counties: Washington County (est. 1788, southeastern Ohio) or Hamilton County (est. 1790, southwestern Ohio). Boundary changes were frequent after 1800 — always work back to these two counties for 1790 events.

**Three land-grant systems:** (1) Virginia Military District (Scioto/Little Miami rivers) — metes-and-bounds, warrants at Virginia State Library; (2) Connecticut Western Reserve (NE Ohio) — records at Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland; (3) U.S. Public Land Survey — remainder, patents at BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov). Source: [Ohio Genealogy — Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)

### Available Records

**Land Records (primary source):**
- Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840 — Collection [1542187](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187) — 234,567 records
- Territorial Land Records, 1788–1799 — Image Group 005112233 — 51 images — ⚠️ Browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text searchable)

**Tax Records:**
- Washington County Tax Records, 1799–1803 — Image Group 005112240 — 73 images, 12% indexed
- Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850 — Collection [1987542](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542) — 345,890 records

**Marriage Records:**
- Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013 — Collection [1803785](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785) — 1,523,678 records

**Church Records (primary vital source):**
- Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950 — Collection [2246917](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917) — 678,234 records
- No civil vital registration existed in 1790; church records are the sole substitute for births and deaths

**Census:** 1790 federal census coverage of the Northwest Territory was sparse. 1800 federal census is the first meaningful enumeration.

**Military:** Northwest Indian War (1785–1795) pension/service records at NARA and Fold3 are a major source class.

**Death Records — GAP:** Collection 1417891 starts 1840. No death record coverage for 1790.

**Probate/Court:** No digitized volumes found for 1780–1810. Physical records at Ohio History Connection, Columbus.

### Key Repositories
- Ohio History Connection, Columbus, OH — territorial court and land records
- Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland, OH — Connecticut Western Reserve records
- Virginia State Library, Richmond, VA — Virginia Military District warrants
- BLM GLO Records (glorecords.blm.gov) — federal patents
- NARA (archives.gov) / Fold3 — military records

---

# 🏅 Locality Guide: California — Gold Rush Era (1848–1865)

## Jurisdictional Overview

California was seized from Mexico in 1846, governed briefly by U.S. military authority, and admitted as a state on September 9, 1850 — **bypassing territorial status entirely**, which means there are no territorial records. The Gold Rush (1848–1855) drew approximately 300,000 people from across the United States and the world. (*Wikipedia: California Gold Rush*)

Civil record-keeping was thin in the early 1850s, especially in the Sierra Nevada foothills mining counties. Infrastructure improved as the decade progressed and the population stabilized.

**County boundary warning:** California's original 27 counties (formed 1850) were subdivided frequently throughout the decade. Mining-country counties — El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Amador — shifted boundaries multiple times. Confirm which county held jurisdiction for a specific place and year *before* searching county-level records.

---

## Records by Type

### 🟢 1. California State Census, 1850–1852
**Digitization level: Indexed + images | 88% name-indexed, full-text searchable**

This is your single most important source for the Gold Rush period. FamilySearch holds 522 images (imageGroupNumber: 006601001), 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable. The 1852 enumeration was taken specifically because California's population was in such flux.

➡ Search free at FamilySearch.org

---

### 🟢 2. U.S. Federal Census, 1850 & 1860
**Digitization level: Indexed + images**

Both enumerations are indexed on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch. **Critical gap: the 1850 federal census for California was partially destroyed — returns for some counties are missing entirely.** Use the 1852 state census as the primary substitute for missing 1850 county returns. (*FamilySearch Wiki: [California Genealogy – Pre-Statehood Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records)*)

**Mortality schedules** (1850, 1860) list individuals who died in the year preceding the census and are often the only death record for Gold Rush-era fatalities.

---

### 🟢 3. County Birth Records, 1850–1919
**Digitization level: Indexed + images**

FamilySearch collection [California, County Births, 1850–1919](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2017276) — **789,456 records** with images. County-level registration began in 1850, but compliance in remote mining camps was extremely uneven. Do not assume a birth record exists for this period; many births went formally unrecorded.

---

### 🟢 4. County Marriage Records, 1850–1952
**Digitization level: Indexed + images**

FamilySearch collection [California, County Marriages, 1850–1952](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1452832) — **567,890 persons recorded**. Coverage improves through the 1850s as the population stabilized.

---

### 🔴 5. Mining Claim Registers, 1849–1855
**⚠ Browse-only images — 0% name-indexed, NOT full-text searchable**

FamilySearch has digitized San Francisco Mining Claim Registers (1849–1855), 340 images (imageGroupNumber: 006601002). **These must be browsed image by image — no name index, no full-text search.** Original mining claim records for other counties are held at each **county recorder's office** throughout the Mother Lode (El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Amador). (*FamilySearch Wiki: [California Genealogy – Gold Rush Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)*)

---

### 🔴 6. Port Arrival Registers, Sacramento, 1849–1858
**⚠ Browse-only images — 0% name-indexed, NOT full-text searchable**

FamilySearch holds 298 images of Sacramento arrival registers (imageGroupNumber: 006601003). **Browse-only, no search capability.** For indexed San Francisco passenger manifests, use Ancestry.com or contact **NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA** directly — that repository holds the primary San Francisco arrival manifests. (*FamilySearch Wiki: [California Genealogy – Gold Rush Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)*)

**Note:** Miners who came overland by wagon train appear in *no* arrival manifest. Their traces are in trail diaries and journals held at the **California State Library** (Sacramento) and the **Bancroft Library** (UC Berkeley).

---

### 🟢 7. Great Registers (Voter Registration), 1866–1910
**Digitization level: Indexed + images** *(begins after target period — essential follow-on source)*

FamilySearch collection [California, Great Registers, 1866–1910](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1923340) — **1,345,678 records**. Entries typically include name, age, nativity, occupation, county of residence, and physical description. Though they begin in 1866, they are indispensable for confirming that a man stayed in California after the rush and for establishing his origins.

---

### 🟡 8. Federal Land Patents
**Digitization level: Indexed and searchable online**

California is a federal public-land state. Patents are searchable free at the [BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov)](https://glorecords.blm.gov). Many mining-district patents date from the late 1850s–1860s as federal surveys opened the land. County deed records (private transfers) are at county courthouses and generally undigitized for this era.

---

### 🔵 9. Military Records
**Digitization level: Partially digitized at Fold3 and NARA**

- **Mexican-American War veterans** who settled in California after 1848: pension files and bounty land warrants at NARA (also on Fold3.com)
- **California volunteer regiments** (Civil War era, western service): muster rolls at NARA and the California State Military Museum
- State militia records for the 1850s are at the **California State Archives**

---

### 🔵 10. Newspapers
**Digitization level: Partially digitized online**

Gold Rush newspapers are genealogically rich and underused. The *Alta California* (San Francisco) and *Sacramento Union* published arrival notices, death notices, mining partnership announcements, and legal notices. Search:
- **Newspapers.com** (subscription)
- **California Digital Newspaper Collection (CDNC)** at UC Riverside — free online

---

### 🔵 11. Probate & Court Records
**Digitization level: Mostly physical at county courthouses**

For transient miners, probate files may be the only record naming relatives back in the home state. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in *any* court of record — state or federal; naturalization files from California's early district courts are at **NARA San Bruno**.

---

### 🔵 12. Church Records
**Digitization level: Varies; many undigitized**

Catholic parishes in San Francisco, Sacramento, and Los Angeles maintained registers from the early American period. Protestant congregations followed the mining population but records survive unevenly. Check denominational archives and contact individual parishes. FamilySearch microfilm coverage for California church records in the 1850s is thin.

---

### 🔵 13. Mission Records, 1769–1850
**Digitization level: Indexed + images** *(background context — pre-dates Gold Rush arrivals)*

FamilySearch collection [California, Mission Records, 1769–1850](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1804372) — **98,765 records**. These cover baptisms, marriages, and burials from the Franciscan mission system. Relevant for California's indigenous and Catholic Hispanic families, not for migrants arriving from 1848 onward.

---

## Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | County births & marriages, state census, Great Registers, mission records, browse-only volumes | Free online |
| **NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA** | San Francisco passenger manifests, federal court naturalizations | In-person; some on Ancestry |
| **California State Archives, Sacramento** | State records, militia rolls, early court records | In-person; some via California Digital Archives |
| **California State Library, Sacramento** | Gold Rush manuscripts, diaries, trail journals, newspapers | In-person |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Largest Gold Rush manuscript collection; mining company records, diaries, letters | In-person |
| **County Recorders / Courthouses** | Mining claims, deeds, probate, pre-1906 naturalizations | In-person; some on Ancestry |
| **Ancestry.com** | 1850 & 1860 census, indexed passenger lists, military pension records | Subscription |
| **Fold3.com** | Military service records, pension files | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com / CDNC** | Historical California newspapers | Subscription / Free |
| **BLM GLO** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery transcriptions | Free |

---

## Key Research Quirks

1. **1850 federal census has gaps.** Some county returns were destroyed. Use the 1852 California State Census (88% indexed on FamilySearch) as your primary fallback.

2. **Mining claim registers and port arrival registers are browse-only.** Both FamilySearch volumes (imageGroupNumbers 006601002 and 006601003) are 0% indexed and not full-text searchable — budget time to browse page by page, or go directly to county recorders and NARA San Bruno respectively.

3. **Civil birth registration was unreliable in mining camps.** County registration existed from 1850 but compliance was erratic in remote districts. Supplement with church records, newspapers, and probate inventories.

4. **County boundaries shifted constantly in the 1850s.** A location in El Dorado County in 1850 might fall under Amador or Alpine County by 1855. Verify jurisdiction by year before pulling county records.

5. **Overland migrants leave no arrival record.** If your ancestor came by wagon train, ship manifests won't help. Look for diaries and journals at the California State Library and Bancroft Library.

6. **Great Registers don't start until 1866.** But they're the best single post-rush source for men who stayed — rich in biographical detail.

7. **Diverse origins demand multilingual thinking.** California's Gold Rush brought large Chinese, Chilean, Mexican, French, German, and Australian communities. Chinese immigrants in particular have a distinct record trail: NARA passenger manifests, later Chinese Exclusion Act files (post-1882), and the Chinese Historical Society of America (San Francisco).

8. **Volume search returned 14 digitized volumes** covering this period, but only the first page (3 volumes) was retrieved here. A follow-up paginated search may surface additional digitized record sets not listed above.

---

## Suggested Starting Sequence

1. **1852 California State Census** (FamilySearch, 88% indexed) — best Gold Rush population snapshot
2. **1850 & 1860 federal census** — with awareness of 1850 county gaps
3. **County births and marriages** on FamilySearch if your ancestor settled
4. **Great Registers from 1866** to confirm he stayed and learn his origins
5. **San Francisco passenger lists** (NARA San Bruno / Ancestry.com) for sea arrivals
6. **BLM GLO** for land patents if he claimed property
7. **Bancroft Library or California State Library** for manuscript collections if you know the specific mining district
8. **Gold Rush-era newspapers** (Newspapers.com, CDNC) for death notices, partnership filings, and community notices

# Locality Guide: New York City (1700s Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Dutch colony of New Amsterdam established 1626; seized by England in 1664 and renamed New York. Throughout the 1700s the city operated under British colonial rule as the administrative center of the Province of New York. (Wikipedia tool result)
- **Geographic scope in the 1700s:** "New York City" in this period meant Manhattan Island — governed as **New York County**. The areas now making up Brooklyn (Kings County), Queens (Queens County), Staten Island (Richmond County), and the Bronx (partly Westchester County) were entirely separate county jurisdictions. Records for families in those areas are filed under their respective counties, not under New York County.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City (Manhattan)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of New York (British Crown, 1664–1776) → State of New York (1776/1783)
- **Population during period:** No figures returned by the population tool for this period.
- **Economy:** Major commercial port and trading center (Wikipedia tool result)
- **Ethnic composition:** Legacy Dutch settler community, English colonists, and other European immigrants (Wikipedia tool result)
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed, Anglican (Church of England / Trinity Church), Presbyterian (Wikipedia tool result; [New York City Genealogy – Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Key historical events:** English takeover 1664 (background); French and Indian War (1754–1763); Revolutionary War — British occupied New York City 1776–1783

## Boundary changes
- In the 1700s, "New York City" = New York County (Manhattan) only. The modern five-borough consolidation did not happen until 1898.
- Families in Kings, Queens, Richmond, or Westchester Counties had records generated and held under those county jurisdictions — not New York County. Confirm your ancestor's specific location before searching.
- The British occupation of the city (1776–1783) disrupted some civil record-keeping during the Revolutionary War years. Verify collection coverage for that specific window.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in New York City during the 1700s colonial period. Church registers are the primary — and often the only — vital record source for this era.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers (see Church Records below).

### Church records — **THE primary vital record source for the 1700s**
- **Dutch Reformed Church Registers, 1700–1776:** One digitized volume confirmed on FamilySearch, imageGroupNumber **007733180**, 211 images, covering New York City 1700–1776. This volume is **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. Records are in **Dutch** and must be read in the original language. (volume_search result)
- **Broader New York church records:** FamilySearch collection **"New York, Church Records, 1640–1940"** (collection ID [1469062](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062)) spans the full 1700s window across multiple denominations. — *Indexed + images*
- **Other key denominations:** Anglican (Trinity Church) and Presbyterian records are specifically identified as major colonial sources. ([New York City Genealogy – Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (online); church archives; New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS); New-York Historical Society. ([New York City Genealogy – Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Language note:** Dutch Reformed records are in Dutch through the mid-1700s; be prepared to read or seek translation help.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census (1790) falls after the colonial period closes. It does not cover the 1700s research window.
- **Colonial-period substitutes:** Tax assessment lists and militia rolls are the best population substitutes — they identify residents ward-by-ward and serve in place of a census for this era. (See Tax Records and Military Records below.)

### Probate and court records
- **Prerogative Court of New York (colonial):** Colonial-period wills were proved before this court. They are indexed in the ***Abstracts of Wills*** series published by the New-York Historical Society — an essential printed finding aid for 1700s probate research. ([New York City Genealogy – Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records))
- **FamilySearch collection:** **"New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971"** (collection ID [1542780](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780)) covers the full 1700s window. — *Indexed + images*
- **Mayor's Court:** Court records of the colonial-era Mayor's Court are a key primary source for the city. ([New York City Genealogy – Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Testate vs. intestate:** For those who left wills (testate), search the *Abstracts of Wills* index and the Probate Records collection. For those who died intestate, look for administration records in the same collections.

### Land records
- **FamilySearch collection:** **"New York, Land Records, 1630–1975"** (collection ID [2078654](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654)) covers the full 1700s window and includes land conveyances. — *Indexed + images*
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts:** Held at the New York State Archives; the primary repository for colonial-era land grants and patents issued by the Province of New York. ([New York City Genealogy – Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial-era grants and patents).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** State-land state — original colonial patents issued by the Crown/Province; held at the New York State Archives.

### Military records
- **Colonial militia rolls:** Militia rolls listing men of military age survive and are a useful tool for identifying colonial-period residents. ([New York City Genealogy – Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records))
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754–1763); American Revolutionary War (1775–1783)
- **Where held:** Fold3 (military records); NARA (National Archives). (external_links_search results)

### Tax records
- **Colonial tax assessment lists:** Ward-level tax lists survive for some years during the colonial period — the most useful census substitute for 1700s New York City. ([New York City Genealogy – Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records))
- **FamilySearch collection (end of period only):** **"New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804"** (collection ID [1678432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432)) covers only 1799–1804 — at the very end of the target window.

### Cemetery records
- **FindAGrave:** Curated as an external cemetery records resource. ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/))
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers for colonial-era churches are likely held by their respective church archives and historical societies.

### Newspaper records
- **New York Gazette:** A colonial-era newspaper identified as a key source containing marriage notices, obituaries, and legal notices. (Wikipedia tool result)
- **Newspapers.com:** Listed as a resource for historical newspapers. ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/))

### Immigration / emigration records
- **Relevant port:** New York City was itself the major port of entry for the colonial period.
- **NARA:** Holds passenger lists and naturalization records. ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/))
- **Coverage note:** Pre-federal passenger records are fragmentary; many colonial arrivals are undocumented in surviving lists. Naturalization before 1906 could be filed in any court of record.

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |

| FamilySearch | New York, Church Records 1640–1940 ([1469062](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062)); Land Records 1630–1975 ([2078654](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654)); Probate Records 1629–1971 ([1542780](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780)); Dutch Reformed Church Registers 1700–1776 vol. 007733180 (browse-only, Dutch); Tax Assessment Rolls 1799–1804 ([1678432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432)) | Free |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |

| New York State Archives | New York Colonial Manuscripts; provincial land grants; administrative records | In-person / online finding aids |
| New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS) | Extensive colonial-era collections | Member access / in-person |
| New-York Historical Society | Colonial-era collections; *Abstracts of Wills* series (indexed finding aid for colonial probate) | In-person / online catalog |

---

## Records NOT online
- **Mayor's Court records** — identified as a key colonial source but not found as a digitized or indexed online collection in the tool results
- **Full run of colonial-era ward tax assessment lists** — only 1799–1804 is in the FamilySearch indexed collection; earlier lists (where they survive) are likely physical/archival
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts** at the New York State Archives — physical/archival; not found as a digitized online collection

---

## Known record losses
- **British occupation (1776–1783):** The Revolutionary War-era occupation disrupted civil record-keeping in the city. Verify collection coverage specifically for the 1776–1783 window.
- **Dutch Reformed Church volume coverage:** The single confirmed digitized volume (007733180) runs 1700–1776. Coverage of other denominations and of the post-1776 period online may be incomplete.

---

## Research tips
- **Church records are your vital record source.** No civil registration existed in 1700s New York. Baptism, marriage, and burial registers — across Dutch Reformed, Anglican, and Presbyterian congregations — are the only vital-event sources. Identify your family's denomination first. ([New York City Genealogy – Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **The Dutch Reformed Church volume is browse-only and in Dutch.** Volume 007733180 is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. Browse image-by-image and read the original Dutch — or seek a translation resource. ([New York City Genealogy – Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Confirm the correct county before searching.** 1700s NYC = New York County (Manhattan) only. Families in Brooklyn (Kings Co.), Queens (Queens Co.), Staten Island (Richmond Co.), or the Bronx (Westchester Co. in part) had their records filed under those separate county jurisdictions — searching "New York County" will miss them.
- **Use the *Abstracts of Wills* series for colonial probate.** Wills proved before the Prerogative Court of New York are indexed in this printed series at the New-York Historical Society — a critical finding aid for 1700s estates. ([New York City Genealogy – Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records))
- **Tax lists and militia rolls substitute for the missing census.** No federal census existed until 1790; ward-level tax assessments and militia rolls are the main tools for locating residents in the 1700s. ([New York City Genealogy – Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records))
- **The NYGBS and New-York Historical Society are essential.** Both hold extensive colonial-era collections that are not fully digitized online. Plan to consult them for any serious colonial NYC research. ([New York City Genealogy – Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives** are the primary source for provincial-era land grants, patents, and administrative records — essential for land and property research. ([New York City Genealogy – Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))

# Locality Research Guide
## Virginia — American Revolutionary War Period (1775–1783)
### Focus: Military Service & Wartime Activities

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies and became a state in 1788. During the Revolutionary War it functioned as both a Commonwealth and a war-making entity, maintaining its own militia, navy, and bounty-land program alongside the Continental Army. **Record-keeping was entirely county-based** — no statewide civil registration existed in this period. Knowing which county your ancestor lived in is therefore the single most important prerequisite before searching. County boundaries shifted frequently in the 18th century as new counties were carved from older ones; when a county of origin is uncertain, work through tax lists and court order books to establish it.

**Critical gap — 1790 federal census:** Virginia's 1790 federal census was destroyed. The 1782–1787 state personal property and land tax lists are the primary substitute and are among the most important wartime documents for the state.

---

## 1. Military Service Records

### Continental Army — Service Records & Muster Rolls
- **Repository:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), Record Group 93 (War Department Collection of Revolutionary War Records)
- **What's there:** Compiled service records and muster rolls for Virginia soldiers in the Continental Line. These are the core documents proving that a man served.
- **Access:** NARA in Washington, DC; also heavily digitized on **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)) — search "Revolutionary War" under military records.
- **Source:** [Virginia Military Records — FamilySearch Wiki, §Revolutionary War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)

### Virginia Militia Records
- **Repository:** Library of Virginia (LVA), Richmond, VA — the primary state archives for Virginia militia records.
- **What's there:** Muster rolls, pay vouchers, and orders for the Virginia state militia, which operated separately from the Continental Line. Many men who do not appear in NARA records will appear in LVA militia holdings.
- **Access:** On-site at the Library of Virginia; some records have been microfilmed by FamilySearch. Contact the LVA reference desk before visiting: [lva.virginia.gov](https://www.lva.virginia.gov).
- **Source:** [Virginia Military Records — FamilySearch Wiki, §Revolutionary War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)

### Virginia State Navy Records
- **Repository:** Library of Virginia, Richmond
- **What's there:** Service records for men who served in Virginia's own naval forces on rivers and coastal waters — a distinct class of service from the Continental Navy and often overlooked.
- **Access:** LVA; also check the published *Virginia State Navy* volumes available in major genealogical libraries.
- **Source:** [Virginia Military Records — FamilySearch Wiki, §Revolutionary War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)

### FamilySearch Digitized Military Collection
- **Collection:** *Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783* (FamilySearch collection ID 1945678)
- **URL:** [familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678)
- **Digitization level:** Name-indexed (returned by `collections_search` as an indexed collection); images present.

---

## 2. Pension & Bounty-Land Records

### Federal Pension & Bounty-Land Warrant Applications
- **Repository:** NARA, Record Group 15 (Records of the Department of Veterans Affairs)
- **What's there:** This is frequently the richest single record class for Revolutionary War research. Pension application files often contain sworn affidavits naming fellow soldiers, describing battles, and including family details (marriage dates, children's names). Widow's pension applications are especially valuable — they can document a marriage that predates most other surviving records.
- **Access:** Microfilmed by NARA (M804 — *Revolutionary War Pension and Bounty-Land Warrant Application Files*, 2,670 rolls); widely available on **Fold3** and **Ancestry** ([ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com)). The full files (not just the index cards) are the ones worth examining.
- **FamilySearch external link:** [NARA — archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/) (returned by `external_links_search`)

### Virginia Bounty Land — Virginia Military District of Ohio
- **Repository:** Virginia State Library (Library of Virginia); also Ohio-side records at the Ohio Historical Society
- **What's there:** Virginia granted bounty land in a reserved tract in present-day Ohio to its veterans. Warrant and survey records connect a soldier's name to his documented service and often record the names of heirs when a veteran died before claiming his land.
- **Access:** Library of Virginia; some records microfilmed by FamilySearch.
- **Source:** [Virginia Military Records — FamilySearch Wiki, §Post-War Bounty Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)

---

## 3. Tax Lists (Critical Substitute for Missing 1790 Census)

- **Collection:** *Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850* (FamilySearch collection ID 1456723)
- **URL:** [familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456823)
- **Digitization level:** Name-indexed with images (returned as an indexed collection by `collections_search`).
- **What's there:** Personal property and land tax lists compiled by county, 1782–1787 and continuing. These lists name adult white males (and in some lists free Black heads of household), document taxable property including enslaved people and livestock, and are the **best available substitute for the destroyed 1790 Virginia census**. They also bracket service dates — a man appearing in 1780 and 1784 lists but absent in between may have been away on service.
- **Quirk:** Lists are organized by county; you must know or narrow down the county to use them efficiently.

---

## 4. Land, Marriage & Will Records

- **Collection:** *Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900* (FamilySearch collection ID 1734285)
- **URL:** [familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285)
- **Digitization level:** Name-indexed with images.
- **What's there:** Wartime wills, deeds, and marriage bonds filed at the county courthouse. Wills made during the war frequently mention military debts or service. Land grants issued during or immediately after the war may connect a man to specific wartime activities. Marriage bonds name a surety (often a family member or neighbor) and are often the only marriage record for this period.

---

## 5. County Court Records

- **Collection:** *Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920* (FamilySearch collection ID 2134567)
- **URL:** [familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567)
- **Digitization level:** Name-indexed with images.
- **What's there:** County court order books are the workhorse record for this period. They document indentures, estates, road orders, militia appointments, loyalist property confiscations, and the business of local government throughout the war. Many Loyalist (Tory) land confiscation records survive only in these books.

---

## 6. Church Records

- **Collection:** *Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929* (FamilySearch collection ID 1598230)
- **URL:** [familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230)
- **Digitization level:** Name-indexed with images.
- **What's there:** Before the Revolution, the Anglican (Church of England) vestry was both a religious and civil authority — it kept birth/baptism, marriage, and burial registers and administered poor relief. After the Disestablishment Act of 1786, parishes lost civil authority and records fragmented across Anglican, Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian congregations. **For the war years themselves (1775–1783), Anglican vestry registers are often the only surviving vital record.** Post-war Baptist and Methodist registers become increasingly important.
- **Quirk:** Many Virginia Anglican vestry books were lost or damaged. When a vestry register is missing, substitute with county court marriage bonds and will abstracts.

---

## 7. Newspapers

- **Repository/Access:** **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)) and the **Library of Virginia's Virginia Chronicle** (free, at [virginiachronicle.com](https://virginiachronicle.com))
- **What's there:** Virginia had active newspapers during the war, especially the *Virginia Gazette* (Williamsburg), which published military appointments, deserter notices, estate notices, and legislative proceedings. A man's name in a deserter advertisement or a military appointment notice is primary documentary evidence of service.
- **FamilySearch external link:** Newspapers.com returned by `external_links_search`.

---

## 8. Cemetery Records

- **Repository/Access:** **Find A Grave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/)) — returned by `external_links_search`
- **What's there:** Many Virginia Revolutionary War soldiers are buried in marked graves with DAR or government markers. Tombstone inscriptions sometimes give regiment or rank. Useful for confirming death dates and locating the county of final residence.

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Library of Virginia** (Richmond) | State militia records, county records on microfilm, published abstracts | On-site + [lva.virginia.gov](https://www.lva.virginia.gov) |
| **NARA** (Washington, DC) | Continental Army service records (RG 93), pension/bounty-land files (RG 15) | On-site; Fold3; Ancestry |
| **FamilySearch** | Digitized collections 1945678, 1734285, 1598230, 1456723, 2134567 | [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) (free) |

# Locality Guide: New Orleans (Orleans Parish), Louisiana (c. 1800–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Founded:** New Orleans 1718 (French); Orleans Parish established 1807 as one of Louisiana's original 19 civil parishes
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Orleans Territory (U.S.) 1803–1812; Louisiana (state) from 1812
- **Economy:** The nation's leading port city; cotton and sugar trade; slave market
- **Ethnic composition:** French and Spanish Creoles, Americans (post-Purchase), enslaved Africans, free people of color (*gens de couleur libres*), Caribbean immigrants, growing Irish and German communities from the 1830s
- **Religion:** Predominantly Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral); Protestant denominations after 1803; Jewish congregations by the 1820s
- **Civil law system:** Louisiana operates under the Napoleonic Code — parishes instead of counties; notarial records are legally foundational; estates are "successions," not "probate"

## Boundary / sovereignty changes

Because New Orleans passed through four sovereignties, records are multilingual and filed under different administrative systems. Search each era's series separately:

| Period | Sovereignty | Record language |
|---|---|---|
| 1718–1763 | French colonial | French, Latin |
| 1763–1800 | Spanish colonial (Cabildo) | Spanish, French |
| 1800–1803 | French again (briefly) | French |
| 1803–1812 | U.S. Territory of Orleans | English, French |
| 1812– | State of Louisiana; Orleans Parish (formed 1807) | English, French |

---

## Known record losses — disasters and what survived

This is the central question for early New Orleans research.

### Great Fire of 1788 (March 21)
Destroyed ~856 of 1,100 buildings in the French Quarter. Most French colonial **civil** records perished. *(Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans)*

### Second Great Fire of 1794 (December 8)
Destroyed ~212 additional buildings, wiping out remaining colonial record fragments. *(Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans)*

### Recurring floods and hurricanes (throughout 1800–1850)
New Orleans' below-sea-level geography made archival flooding a chronic hazard. Records in low-lying buildings were repeatedly at risk.

### Yellow fever epidemics
Recurring throughout the early 1800s. These events disrupted institutions but also generated mortality records — death registers, Charity Hospital records, cemetery sexton records — that help substitute for the missing civil registration.

### The key survival fact
**The fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed records created before 1800 — not the early 1800s records themselves.** The notarial archives survived because Louisiana's civil law required notaries to maintain their own personal registers, housed separately from government offices. For your target period of 1800–1850, record survival is actually relatively good by the standards of the era. The table below shows what was lost, what survived, and where substitutes live:

| Disaster | Date | Records lost | Best substitutes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Great Fire of 1788 | Mar. 21, 1788 | Most French colonial civil records | St. Louis Cathedral registers; notarial archives; Spanish Cabildo records |
| Second Great Fire of 1794 | Dec. 8, 1794 | Remaining colonial records | Same as above; Spanish land grant files |
| Floods / hurricanes | Throughout 1800–1850 | Sporadic archival damage | Cross-reference notarial acts with church registers; seek multiple-party copies |
| Epidemic disruptions | Recurring 1800s | Some institutional records | Church death registers; Charity Hospital records; cemetery sexton records |

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration) — CRITICAL GAP
Louisiana had **no statewide civil vital registration** during 1800–1850. Statewide registration did not begin until **1914**. For this entire period, church sacramental registers are the primary vital records source — not civil registration.

- Civil marriage registration at the parish level existed sporadically; consistent civil marriage records begin around **1837**.
- **FamilySearch — Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957** (collection [1798054](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1798054); ~567,890 records, ~283,945 images; **indexed + images**) — covers only the tail end of the 1800–1850 window.
- **FamilySearch — Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964** (collection [1543892](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892); ~2,345,678 index entries; **index only — zero images online**) — useful for leads, but you must request original documents from the Louisiana State Archives.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge); Orleans Parish Clerk of Court.

---

### Church records ← PRIMARY SOURCE for 1800–1850

St. Louis Cathedral's sacramental registers survive from **1731**, with gaps for the fire periods, and are the single most important genealogical source for this place and period.

- **FamilySearch — Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925** (collection [1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905); ~987,654 records, ~493,827 images; **indexed + images**) — the main online access point for St. Louis Cathedral and other Louisiana church registers.
- **Separate registers:** St. Louis Cathedral maintained *distinct* sacramental registers for (1) white parishioners, (2) free people of color (*gens de couleur libres*), and (3) enslaved persons. All three sets survive and are included in the FamilySearch collection. For African American research this is essential.
- **Language:** Latin, French, and (pre-1803) Spanish; shifting toward English after 1803.
- **Protestant congregation records** (Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist) are held at individual churches and denominational archives — largely not digitized.
- **Physical:** Archives of the Archdiocese of New Orleans; many registers also on FamilySearch microfilm.

*(FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)*

---

### Notarial records ← UNIQUE TO LOUISIANA; ESSENTIAL SUBSTITUTE

Louisiana's civil law required virtually every significant legal transaction — property sales, wills, contracts, successions, mortgages, manumissions of enslaved persons, marriage contracts, apprenticeships — to be executed before a notary and recorded in the notary's personal register. These registers survived the fires of 1788 and 1794 precisely because they were housed with the notaries themselves, not in government buildings.

- **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** (421 Loyola Ave, New Orleans) holds over **30 million pages** of notarial acts dating back to 1734. This is the richest surviving genealogical archive for the city.
- **FamilySearch volume 004990115** — 167 browse-only images of surviving notarial microfilm copies, Orleans Parish, **1803–1820**. **Digitization level: browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; bilingual French/English). Must be browsed image by image.
- **What these records contain:** Wills, property sales, marriage contracts, manumissions, powers of attorney, business agreements — all naming parties, witnesses, addresses, and often family relationships.
- **Language:** French, Spanish (pre-1803), English (increasingly post-1803).

*(FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)*

---

### Successions (probate) and civil law records

Louisiana's civil-law equivalent of probate is the **succession**. Related record types: **tutorship** (guardianship of minors), **interdiction** (incapacity proceedings). These are the terms to search — not "probate," "guardianship," or "will."

- **FamilySearch — Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984** (collection [2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341); ~456,789 records, ~228,394 images; **indexed + images**) — covers the full target period.
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court; Louisiana State Archives.
- **Value:** Successions name heirs, creditors, and often enumerate property including enslaved persons — invaluable when vital records are missing.

*(FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System)*

---

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Orleans Parish appears in **1810, 1820, 1830, and 1840**. The 1800 federal census for Louisiana Territory has very limited survival. The 1820 and later censuses list free colored persons separately; 1840 lists pension recipients by name.
- **Access:** **Indexed + images** on both FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry.com (subscription).

---

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French/Spanish long-lot (*arpent*) system — not the rectangular township-and-range grid used elsewhere in the U.S.
- **Pre-1803 Spanish and French land grants** were confirmed under American authority; files in the *American State Papers, Public Lands* series (online at memory.loc.gov).
- **Federal land patents post-1803:** BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) — free, searchable online.
- **Deeds and conveyances:** Orleans Parish Notarial Archives and the Conveyance Office of Orleans Parish — largely physical only.

---

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 / Battle of New Orleans (1815); Mexican-American War (1846–48).
- **Access:** Fold3.com (subscription; **indexed + images**); NARA (archives.gov).

---

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (est. 1789); St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (est. 1823); Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 (est. 1833).
- **Online:** FindAGrave.com (free; substantial New Orleans coverage).
- **Physical:** Burial registers at the Archdiocese of New Orleans and individual cemetery offices.
- **Note:** New Orleans uses above-ground tombs because of the water table. **Burial registers, not headstone inscriptions, are the primary genealogical source.**

---

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** *Le Moniteur de la Louisiane* (founded 1794), *Louisiana Gazette* (1804), *New Orleans Picayune* (1837). Carry death notices, marriage announcements, estate sale notices, legal advertisements.
- **Access:** Newspapers.com (subscription); **Chronicling America** at chroniclingamerica.loc.gov (free; some Louisiana papers digitized); Louisiana State University Libraries (microfilm).

---

### Immigration / passenger records
- New Orleans was one of the busiest U.S. ports. **Customs passenger arrival lists survive from 1813** (NARA, RG 36).
- **Access:** Ancestry.com has indexed passenger lists for New Orleans 1813–1963 (**indexed + images**, subscription). NARA holds originals.
- Large Irish and German immigration peaked in the 1830s–1840s; earlier passengers include French, Spanish, and Caribbean arrivals.

---

### Tax records
- **Orleans Parish assessment rolls** at the Louisiana State Archives — **physical only**.
- **Substitute value:** These rolls can place a person in the parish for **1800–1809**, before consistent federal census coverage for Louisiana begins.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1718–1925 (1612905); Parish Marriages 1837–1957 (1798054); Probate Records 1756–1984 (2078341); Death Index 1819–1964 (1543892); Notarial Acts 1803–1820, browse-only (vol. 004990115) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Federal census; passenger lists 1813–1963 | Subscription |
| Fold3.com | Military service, pension, draft records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave.com | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (loc.gov) | Historic Louisiana newspapers | Free |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents post-1803 | Free |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center, 421 Loyola Ave | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person; appointment recommended |
| Archives of the Archdiocese of New Orleans | St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers; diocesan records | In-person; many on FamilySearch microfilm |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial records; state vital records; court records | In-person; some online |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Succession, tutorship, interdiction, court records | In-person |
| Historic New Orleans Collection, 533 Royal St | Manuscripts, maps, newspapers, photographs | In-person; free |
| Louisiana State Museum / Louisiana Historical Center | Cabildo (Spanish colonial) records; colonial manuscripts | In-person |
| Tulane University Special Collections | Louisiana and New Orleans manuscripts | In-person |

---

## Records NOT online
- Most notarial acts outside the FamilySearch 1803–1820 browse-only volume (the 30+ million page archive is largely undigitized)
- Original death register images underlying the Statewide Death Index 1819–1964 (index is online; originals are not)
- Orleans Parish assessment / tax rolls
- Tutorship and interdiction records (Civil District Court)
- Spanish Cabildo administrative records
- Most Protestant congregation registers
- Charity Hospital of New Orleans records (at Louisiana State Archives; not digitized)

---

## Research tips

1. **Start with church records, not civil registration.** Louisiana had no statewide vital registration until 1914. For 1800–1850 baptisms, marriages, and burials, search FamilySearch collection 1612905 first. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))

2. **Use notarial records as your all-purpose substitute.** Virtually every important life event left a notarial trace — wills, marriage contracts, manumissions, property sales. The Notarial Archives Research Center (421 Loyola Ave) is indispensable. FamilySearch volume 004990115 covers 1803–1820 in browse-only form. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))

3. **Search under all four sovereignties.** Records from 1800–1803 may be in French or Spanish administrative systems; 1803 onward shifts to American. Collection 1612905 spans all three eras.

4. **Look for free people of color in separate church registers.** St. Louis Cathedral kept distinct registers for *gens de couleur libres* and enslaved persons — both sets survive and are searchable in collection 1612905.

5. **Use Louisiana civil-law terminology.** Search for "succession," "tutorship," and "interdiction," not "probate," "guardianship," or "will." ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System))

6. **The Statewide Death Index (collection 1543892) is an index only.** No images are online. Use it to pin down a death, then request the original from the Louisiana State Archives.

7. **Check passenger arrival lists.** New Orleans was one of the nation's busiest ports; lists survive from 1813 and are indexed on Ancestry.com and at NARA.

8. **Tax rolls fill the 1800–1809 gap** before reliable federal census coverage. Orleans Parish assessment rolls at the Louisiana State Archives can confirm residence and property.

9. **Plan for multilingual records.** Expect French and Latin in church records, Spanish in pre-1803 notarial acts, and a gradual shift to English post-1803. Build in time for translation.

10. **In-person visits may be unavoidable.** The Historic New Orleans Collection, the Louisiana Historical Center (Cabildo records), and the Notarial Archives Research Center all hold unique materials with no online equivalent.

---

The record counts from the collections tool (987,654; 567,890; etc.) are as returned by FamilySearch and should be treated as approximate figures rather than verified totals. If you want to dig deeper into any specific record type — such as running targeted searches in the church records collection or the notarial volume — just say the word.

- **Parent jurisdiction:** Orleans Territory (U.S.) 1803–1812; Louisiana (state) from 1812

---

## Locality Guide: Boston Port Arrivals, 1840s
**Place:** Boston, Suffolk, Massachusetts, United States
**Period:** 1840–1860 (with some collection coverage extending beyond)

---

### Historical Context

Boston was one of the five major U.S. ports of entry during the 1840s and the primary New England destination for immigrants fleeing the Irish Great Famine (1845–1852). By 1850 more than a quarter of Boston's population was Irish-born. Immigrants settled primarily in the North End and Fort Hill neighborhoods. Records created at arrival were **customs passenger lists** — thinner documents than the later Ellis Island–era manifests, typically recording only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin.

---

### 1. Passenger Arrival Records (The Core Source)

| Record | Access | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891** | Indexed + images on FamilySearch (collection 1784312) and Ancestry | NARA (originals); FamilySearch / Ancestry (online) |
| **Port of Boston image volume (003345210)** | **3% name-indexed; full-text searchable** — not reliably findable by name search alone; images must be browsed or full-text searched | FamilySearch (389 images, 1840–1850) |

**Key facts about 1840s customs lists:**
- Recorded under NARA Record Group 36 (Records of the Bureau of Customs).
- The original physical records are held at the **National Archives at Boston, 380 Trapelo Road, Waltham, MA** — accessible in person.
- The FamilySearch indexed collection (1784312) is your fastest first pass, but indexing errors are common for this period (phonetic variants, anglicised spellings). If a name search fails, browse the image volume (003345210) directly or use full-text search.
- **Ancestry.com** also indexes this series — search both platforms, as their index entries are built independently and one may catch what the other missed.
- 1840s lists do **not** name the port of departure, ship's captain's home port, or relatives joining the immigrant — information that becomes available on post-1895 manifests. Supplement with the sources below to reconstruct origin.

---

### 2. Naturalization Records (Confirming Arrival and Origin)

| Record | Access | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906** | Indexed on FamilySearch (collection 1459213, ~345,000 records) | Suffolk County courts; NARA Boston |

**How these help:**
- An immigrant who arrived in the 1840s would typically file a **Declaration of Intention** ("first papers") within a few years of arrival and a **Petition for Naturalization** 2–5 years later.
- Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in *any* court of record — Suffolk County Court of Common Pleas, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, U.S. Circuit or District Courts all issued them. Search all.
- Naturalization papers sometimes name the ship, exact arrival date, and country/town of birth — far more than the passenger list itself.
- NARA Boston (Waltham) holds original naturalization files from federal courts; the Massachusetts State Archives holds state-court originals.

---

### 3. Church Records (Vital Events After Arrival)

| Record | Access | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920** | Indexed on FamilySearch (collection 1921657, ~987,000 records) | Various; Archdiocese of Boston Archives |

**Key notes for immigrant research:**
- The **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** holds Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) from the 1840s onward, including records from the **Cathedral of the Holy Cross** and **St. Patrick's** — both central to the Irish immigrant community.
- These registers often record the townland or parish of origin in Ireland, information that never appears on customs passenger lists. This is frequently the **only** primary source for an immigrant's specific place of origin.
- Protestant and other denomination records also exist for this period; check the denomination's own archives as well as FamilySearch microfilm.
- Statewide vital registration in Massachusetts began in **1841** at the state level (town clerks had been ordered to record vital events since 1639). Both the state-level series and older town series overlap in this decade — search both.

---

### 4. The Boston Pilot "Missing Persons" Advertisements

This is a unique and important resource specific to Boston Irish immigration:
- *The Pilot*, Boston's Irish Catholic newspaper, published "Missing Persons" advertisements from the 1830s–1920s — notices placed by immigrants (or their families in Ireland) searching for relatives. These ads often state the emigrant's county and townland of origin.
- The database is searchable free online at **[infowanted.bc.edu](http://infowanted.bc.edu)** (Boston College). Searches by surname, county, and year are supported.
- Even if your ancestor didn't place an ad, a sibling or cousin may have — and their notice can unlock the family's origin.

---

### 5. Vital Records After Arrival

| Record | Access | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890** | Indexed on FamilySearch (collection 2061550, ~3.4 million records) | Town clerks; Massachusetts State Archives; FamilySearch |

- Massachusetts statewide registration (begun 1841) means births, marriages, and deaths of immigrant children born in Boston should appear here.
- Records are filed **at the town/city level** — Boston city records are the primary series. Search "Boston" specifically, not just "Suffolk County."

---

### 6. Federal Census Records

- The **1850 federal census** is the first to list every household member by name, age, sex, and birthplace (country for foreign-born). This is a critical anchor: an immigrant who arrived in the 1840s should appear in the 1850 Boston census.
- The **1860 census** adds real estate and personal estate values, useful for tracking immigrant economic progress.
- Neither 1850 nor 1860 records the specific arrival year or ship — but birthplace of children (whether Massachusetts or foreign-born) can help bracket the arrival window.
- Available indexed on FamilySearch, Ancestry, and FamilySearch's free search at familysearch.org.

---

### 7. Other Supporting Records

| Record type | Why relevant | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Probate Records, 1635–1991** (FS collection 1678901) | Wills and estate files name family members and sometimes birthplace | Suffolk County Probate Court; FamilySearch (indexed, ~567,000 records) |
| **Historical newspapers** | Ship arrival notices, obituaries, and community news appeared in Boston dailies | Newspapers.com, GenealogyBank, and the Boston Public Library's digitized holdings |
| **NARA RG 85 (INS records)** | Passenger arrival cards and immigration case files — thin for the 1840s but useful if the individual passed through later | National Archives at Waltham |
| **Massachusetts State Archives** | State-court naturalizations, town clerk birth/death registers, state census schedules | 220 Morrissey Blvd, Boston, MA |
| **Fold3** | Military pension and service records — useful if the immigrant served in the U.S. military post-arrival | fold3.com |

---

### Key Access Gaps and Quirks

- **1840s passenger lists are thin.** They record country of origin (e.g., "Ireland") — not county, parish, or townland. To find the specific origin, you must work forward from this record into church registers, naturalization papers, or *The Pilot* ads.
- **The Port of Boston image volume (003345210) is only 3% name-indexed.** A name search on FamilySearch will miss most entries. Always follow a failed name search with a browse of the images or a full-text search.
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered.** They can appear in any court — Suffolk County, state supreme court, or federal court. Search all three series, not just one.
- **Church records are the key to Irish origins.** Customs passenger lists almost never name a specific townland; Catholic baptismal and marriage registers frequently do. The Archdiocese of Boston Archives is the primary physical repository.
- **Companion records at the port of departure.** Many Irish Famine emigrants left from Liverpool, England rather than directly from Irish ports. If Boston arrival records don't give enough detail, consider searching Liverpool-outbound passenger records (held at The National Archives, Kew, UK, and digitized on Ancestry under "UK, Outward Passenger Lists").

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA)** | Customs passenger lists (originals), federal naturalization records, federal court files |
| **Massachusetts State Archives (Boston)** | State-court naturalizations, town vital records, state censuses |
| **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** | Catholic parish registers for Boston area churches from 1840s onward |
| **Boston Public Library** | Historical newspapers, city directories, local history collections |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Digitized/indexed passenger lists, naturalization records, town vitals, church records, probate |
| **Ancestry.com** | Independent index to the same passenger list series; U.S. censuses |
| **Boston College (infowanted.bc.edu)** | The Pilot Missing Persons database — free, searchable |

---

**Recommended starting sequence:**
1. Search the indexed **Massachusetts Passenger Lists, 1820–1891** (FamilySearch collection 1784312) — then if not found, browse/full-text the image volume 003345210.
2. Anchor the immigrant in the **1850 federal census** (Boston, Suffolk County).
3. Search **naturalization records** (FS collection 1459213) for a Declaration of Intention or Petition — these often give the most biographical detail.
4. Search the **Boston Pilot Missing Persons database** for the surname.
5. Pursue **Catholic parish registers** at the Archdiocese of Boston Archives for the family's baptisms and marriages, which may name the Irish townland of origin.

## Locality Research Guide
### Native American Families in Indian Territory (Present-Day Oklahoma) · ca. 1830–1880

---

### Jurisdictional Context

During the mid-1800s, present-day Oklahoma was **Indian Territory** — not a U.S. state (statehood did not come until 1907) and not organized into counties with civil vital registration. Authority rested with the **Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA)** and the tribal nations themselves. The **Five Civilized Tribes** — Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole — were relocated from the southeastern U.S. under the Indian Removal Act of 1830, many via the Trail of Tears in the 1830s–1840s.

This has two major consequences for genealogical research:
- **No county-level civil birth, marriage, or death records exist for this period.** The record infrastructure that governs research in other U.S. states simply did not exist here until after 1907.
- **Tribal and federal records are the primary genealogical sources** — tribal rolls, BIA agency records, missionary registers, land allotment files, and treaty documents replace the standard vital-record stack.

---

### Record Types, Availability, and Access

---

#### 1. Tribal Enrollment Rolls ⭐ *Start here*

These are the backbone of Native American genealogy in Indian Territory. They function as the region's substitute for vital records and census schedules.

**Pre-Dawes rolls (your primary mid-1800s sources):**

| Roll | Tribe | Date | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Old Settler Cherokee Roll | Cherokee | 1851 | Western Cherokee who had migrated earlier |
| Drennen Roll | Cherokee | 1852 | Eastern Cherokee after removal |
| BIA Annual Annuity Payment Rolls | All Five Tribes | 1830s–1900s | Heads of household; sometimes list family members |

- **Where held:** National Archives at Fort Worth, Texas (Record Group 75, Microfilm M234)
- **Online access:** Partially indexed on FamilySearch and Fold3; coverage is uneven — some volumes must be browsed
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* — 567,890 indexed records, 283,945 images — [familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432)
- **Digitized volume:** Image Group 002298871, Tribal Enrollment Cards 1840–1870 — 940 images, **99% name-indexed and full-text searchable** — high confidence this is reachable via FamilySearch record search

**The Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** fall after the target period but are essential for working backward. Each entry records name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation, and is tied to a census card number and allotment jacket. The age data lets you calculate mid-1800s birth dates. Fully indexed on FamilySearch, Ancestry, and Fold3; held at NARA Fort Worth (RG 75).
- FamilySearch Wiki: [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Dawes\_Rolls](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Dawes_Rolls)
- Pre-Dawes context: [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Dawes\_Rolls#Pre-Dawes](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Dawes_Rolls#Pre-Dawes)

---

#### 2. BIA Agency Records (Annuity Rolls, Correspondence, School Records)

The BIA Indian agents filed annual reports, payment vouchers, and correspondence with tribal leaders. These records often name individuals who do not appear on formal rolls.

- **Annuity payment rolls** (heads of household, sometimes family members) — NARA RG 75, Microfilm M234 — partially indexed on FamilySearch and Fold3
- **School records** — mission and BIA boarding schools list student names, ages, tribal affiliation, and sometimes parents
- **Agency correspondence** — may identify individuals in disputes, land claims, or removal-era actions
- **Where held:** National Archives at Fort Worth; Oklahoma Historical Society
- FamilySearch Wiki: [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five\_Civilized\_Tribes\_Records#Annuity\_Rolls](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records#Annuity_Rolls)

---

#### 3. Land and Allotment Records

- **FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907* — 234,567 records, 117,283 images — [familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872)
- **Allotment jackets** (Dawes-era, but referencing mid-1800s ancestry): each jacket contains maps, legal documents, and correspondence identifying the enrollee's kin network
- **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov) — federal patent records for Indian Territory land cessions
- Tribal land records are also held at individual tribal archives

---

#### 4. Missionary and Church Records

Christian missionaries (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian) established churches and schools among the relocated tribes from the 1820s onward and kept registers of converts, students, marriages, and burials — filling the role that civil vital records play elsewhere.

- **FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965* — 123,456 records, 61,728 images — [familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321)
- **Denominational archives** hold records not yet digitized — check Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian historical societies
- FamilySearch Wiki: [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma\_Native\_American\_Records#Missionary\_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)

---

#### 5. Tribal Court Records

Each of the Five Civilized Tribes maintained its own court system during the Indian Territory period. Tribal court files can include probate actions, guardianship cases, land disputes, and civil suits that name family members.

- **Where held:** Tribal archives (Cherokee Nation Archives in Tahlequah, OK; Choctaw Nation Archives; etc.) and NARA Fort Worth (RG 75)
- Access varies by tribe — contact tribal historic preservation offices directly
- FamilySearch Wiki: [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five\_Civilized\_Tribes\_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records)

---

#### 6. Treaty Documents

Treaties between the U.S. government and tribal nations are primary documents that sometimes list signatories and tribal leadership by name, and always establish the legal context for removal and land ownership.

- **Key mid-1800s treaties:** Treaty of New Echota (1835, Cherokee); Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek (1830, Choctaw); various removal-era agreements
- **Where held:** NARA (Record Group 11 — Ratified Treaties); Oklahoma Historical Society; digitized at [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)
- Not a record of ordinary families, but essential for establishing which band/group an ancestor belonged to

---

#### 7. Federal Census — Special Indian Schedules

Indian Territory residents were **excluded from the regular decennial U.S. federal census** during the mid-1800s. However, special enumeration efforts exist:

- **Indian Population Schedules** were compiled for some years and some territories
- **Tribal censuses** conducted by BIA agents are indexed in FamilySearch's *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls* collection above
- For the 1860 and 1870 federal censuses, check both the main census and any Indian schedules — coverage is partial

---

#### 8. Military Records

The Civil War (1861–1865) split the Five Civilized Tribes, with some nations allying with the Confederacy and others with the Union, producing distinct military service records for Native American units.

- **Service records and pension files:** NARA (Record Group 94); indexed on Fold3 — [fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)
- Indian Home Guard units (Union) and Confederate Cherokee/Choctaw units both generated pension and service documentation
- Post-war Southern Claims Commission records may also name individuals

---

#### 9. Freedmen Records

Tribal members who held enslaved people brought them into Indian Territory. After the Civil War, treaty provisions extended tribal citizenship to Freedmen in some nations, and they appear on tribal rolls (including the Freedmen rolls under Dawes). If your research intersects with African American ancestry in Indian Territory, Freedmen tribal rolls are an essential source — they are part of the same RG 75 holdings at NARA Fort Worth and are indexed in the FamilySearch collections above.

---

#### 10. Newspapers and Other Sources

- **Historical newspapers:** [newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) — Cherokee Phoenix and other tribal newspapers of the period occasionally published names
- **Cemetery records:** [findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/) — many Indian Territory cemetery transcriptions have been contributed
- **Oklahoma Historical Society** — holds manuscript collections, agency records, and photographs not available digitally

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What's There |
|---|---|
| **National Archives at Fort Worth, TX** (RG 75) | BIA agency records, tribal rolls, allotment files, annuity rolls (M234), Dawes rolls |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** (okhistory.org) | Agency correspondence, territorial newspapers, manuscripts |
| **Tribal archives** (Cherokee Nation, Choctaw Nation, etc.) | Tribal court records, council minutes, tribal school records |
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Indexed collections for rolls, land records, mission records; Image Group 002298871 |
| **Ancestry.com** | Dawes Rolls; federal census; cross-indexed with FamilySearch holdings |
| **Fold3** (fold3.com) | Military records; some BIA annuity rolls |
| **NARA online** (archives.gov) | Treaties; federal records not yet on FamilySearch/Ancestry |

---

### Research Quirks and Cautions

1. **No county civil vital records for the mid-1800s.** Indian Territory had no county infrastructure until near statehood (1907). Tribal rolls and missionary registers are the functional equivalent.
2. **Start with the Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) and work backward.** Even though they postdate the target period, the age data, blood quantum, and census card numbers connect directly to mid-1800s ancestors.
3. **Pre-Dawes rolls are inconsistently indexed** — the Old Settler and Drennen rolls, and BIA annuity rolls, will often require browsing microfilm rather than searching by name.
4. **Tribal archives vary in public access.** Contact each nation's historic preservation or cultural resources office before planning a visit or requesting records.
5. **Freedmen research requires checking both African American genealogy resources and tribal rolls** — the two research streams converge in Indian Territory.
6. **The Five Civilized Tribes each had separate records.** Searches must be scoped to the correct nation — a search in Choctaw rolls will not surface Cherokee ancestors.
7. **Indian Territory is the jurisdictional name to use** in FamilySearch catalog searches, not "Oklahoma" — many pre-1907 volumes are cataloged under Indian Territory, United States.

---

### Recommended Search Order

1. **FamilySearch:** *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* → identify tribal affiliation and roll entries
2. **FamilySearch:** Image Group 002298871 (Tribal Enrollment Cards, 1840–1870, 99% indexed)
3. **NARA Fort Worth / Fold3:** BIA annuity rolls (M234) for the relevant agency
4. **FamilySearch:** *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907*
5. **FamilySearch:** *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965*
6. **Tribal archives** for court records, council records, and school registers
7. **Dawes Rolls** (Ancestry/FamilySearch/Fold3) → use ages to project backward to mid-1800s birth events
