---

## Pennsylvania Quaker Research Guide — Late 1700s

**Place:** Pennsylvania, United States | **Period:** c. 1750–1800

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Pennsylvania was founded in 1682 by William Penn as a Quaker haven. By the late 1700s, Quakers (Religious Society of Friends) were heavily concentrated in **Philadelphia County, Chester County, Bucks County, and Delaware County** — the colonial core of the province. Pennsylvania did **not** mandate statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths until **1906**, which means Quaker meeting records are not a supplement to civil registration for this period — **they are effectively the only vital record source** for most Quaker families.

---

### The Quaker Meeting Structure — Why It Matters for Research

Quaker record-keeping followed a formal hierarchy, and knowing where your ancestor's meeting sat in that hierarchy tells you where to look:

| Level | Function | Records Created |
|---|---|---|
| **Preparative meeting** | Local worship gathering | Preparatory minutes (sometimes) |
| **Monthly meeting** | The core record-keeping unit | Births, deaths, marriages, disownments, certificates of removal |
| **Quarterly meeting** | Regional oversight | Quarterly minutes |
| **Yearly meeting** | Annual governance | Yearly meeting minutes |

**Philadelphia Yearly Meeting** was the governing body for Pennsylvania (and surrounding colonies/states) throughout the late 1700s. All research begins by identifying which **monthly meeting** your ancestor attended.

---

### Record Types — What They Contain

**1. Monthly Meeting Registers (Births, Marriages, Deaths)**
Monthly meetings kept separate registers recording:
- **Births** — child's name, parents, date
- **Deaths** — name, date, sometimes age and cause
- **Marriages** — couple's names, date, location, and the names of *all witnesses who signed the certificate* (making Quaker marriage records uniquely rich for identifying extended family networks)

Pennsylvania had no statewide civil vital registration in this period. These registers stand in for that. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)), Quaker records are among the most detailed religious records in Pennsylvania and directly substitute for civil registration.

**2. Certificates of Removal**
When a Quaker family moved from one meeting area to another, the original meeting issued a "certificate of removal" to the receiving meeting. These certificates:
- Name the individual or family being transferred
- State the meeting of origin and meeting of destination
- Certify the person's good standing

For genealogists tracing migration, these are invaluable — they document movement from Pennsylvania to Ohio, Indiana, the Carolinas, and other states in the late 1700s and early 1800s.

**3. Disownment Records**
If a Friend violated community norms (marrying a non-Quaker, marrying outside the meeting, military service, moral offenses), the monthly meeting issued a disownment. The disownment record names the individual and specifies the cause — genealogically useful precisely because it was triggered by a significant life event.

> **Quirk:** If an ancestor disappears from Quaker records around the time of a marriage, check the disownment minutes. Marrying a non-Quaker in a civil ceremony was one of the most common causes of disownment in this period.

**4. Monthly and Yearly Meeting Minutes**
Broader governance proceedings recorded at monthly, quarterly, and yearly levels. FamilySearch holds **1 confirmed digitized volume** of this type:
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800** — image group `001188322`, 145 images
- ⚠️ **Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be viewed image by image.

---

### Repositories

#### 1. Friends Historical Library — Swarthmore College, Swarthmore, PA
The largest collection of American Quaker records in existence, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)). Holds original monthly meeting registers, removal certificates, disownment records, and meeting minutes for Pennsylvania meetings. **This is the primary repository** for the late 1700s period. Many of their holdings have been microfilmed by FamilySearch.
- Website: [www.swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library](https://www.swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library)

#### 2. Quaker and Special Collections — Haverford College, Haverford, PA
A second major repository for Pennsylvania Quaker materials, per Wikipedia's article on Quakers in Pennsylvania. Complements Swarthmore's holdings.
- Website: [www.haverford.edu/quaker-and-special-collections](https://www.haverford.edu/quaker-and-special-collections)

#### 3. FamilySearch — Digitized & Microfilm Holdings
FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania monthly meeting registers. The one confirmed digitized volume in the target window is the **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800** (browse-only). Additional meeting-level volumes may exist on microfilm not yet digitized. Use FamilySearch's [Catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/catalog/search) and search by county + "Friends" or "Quaker" or "Society of Friends" to identify microfilmed registers for specific meetings.

FamilySearch indexed collections overlapping this period (from `collections_search`):
| Collection | Date Range | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 | 1683–1994 | Useful supplement — Quakers did write wills |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 | 1677–1950 | Covers secular/civil marriages |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 | 1700–1900 | Compiled abstracts |

> ⚠️ None of the above are Quaker-specific; the Quaker meeting registers themselves are not yet name-indexed in FamilySearch for this period beyond the browse-only volume noted above.

#### 4. William Wade Hinshaw — *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*
A 6-volume published abstract of meeting records from Pennsylvania and surrounding states, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)). This is the most searchable compiled index of Quaker genealogical records and is widely available in genealogical libraries and on Ancestry.com. It covers births, marriages, deaths, and disownments abstracted from the original registers.

#### 5. Ancestry.com
Ancestry hosts a digitized version of Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia* and some Pennsylvania church/meeting records. No Pennsylvania Quaker-specific collection for 1700–1820 was surfaced by FamilySearch's curated external links tool for this period, but Ancestry's search interface for Pennsylvania records is worth checking directly.

---

### Key Counties and Their Meetings (Late 1700s)

| County | Known Quaker Monthly Meetings | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Philadelphia** | Philadelphia Monthly Meeting, Germantown | Urban center; Philadelphia Yearly Meeting based here |
| **Chester County** | Bradford, Concord, Goshen, Kennett, London Grove, Uwchlan, others | Densest rural Quaker concentration |
| **Bucks County** | Falls, Middletown, Makefield, Wrightstown | Strong Quaker presence from earliest settlement |
| **Delaware County** | Darby, Radnor, Haverford | Core William Penn-era settlements |

---

### Complementary Record Sources for This Period

Since civil registration doesn't exist, pair meeting records with:

- **Land and deed records** (county courthouses / Pennsylvania State Archives) — Quakers transferred land within the community frequently; deeds name relationships
- **Probate/wills** — FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994) covers this period and is indexed
- **Pennsylvania tax lists, 1762–1794** — available at the Pennsylvania State Archives; lists heads of household and taxable property
- **1790 Federal Census** — first enumeration; heads of household only, but places families geographically within a meeting area
- **Pennsylvania Archives (published series)** — abstracts of colonial and early national records, widely available in libraries

---

### Key Research Quirks

1. **Pennsylvania had no statewide civil vital registration until 1906.** Quaker meeting registers are effectively the vital records for this period — don't look for a state birth or death certificate.
2. **Identify the monthly meeting first**, not just the county. A county may have had multiple monthly meetings with separate registers. Wrong meeting = missing the record entirely.
3. **Hinshaw's Encyclopedia is the fastest name-searchable starting point**, but it is an abstract — always go back to the original register or microfilm for the full entry.
4. **Marriage certificates list all witnesses.** A Quaker marriage record can identify a dozen or more family members and neighbors who attended. Don't read only the names of the couple.
5. **Certificates of removal track migration.** If your family moved west or south after 1790, the certificate of removal from their Pennsylvania meeting to the new meeting is often the only record linking the two locations.
6. **Disownment minutes are a research trap and a resource.** A family member who married out, joined the military, or violated discipline may have dropped out of meeting records — but the disownment entry records why and when, preserving the name and date.
7. **The FamilySearch Wiki place-specific pages for Pennsylvania did not return Pennsylvania-specific content** through the survey tool — consult the Wiki directly at [FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records) for the most current guidance.

---

### Digitization Summary

| Record Type | Availability | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800 | Digitized on FamilySearch (145 images) | Browse-only — no index, no full-text |
| Monthly meeting registers (Chester, Bucks, Delaware, Philadelphia) | Microfilmed by FamilySearch; many NOT yet digitized | FamilySearch Catalog → microfilm; or Friends Historical Library in person |
| Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia* (abstracts) | Published; on Ancestry.com | Name-searchable |
| Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994 | Indexed on FamilySearch (collection 1999196) | Searchable by name |
| Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 | On FamilySearch (collection 1502909) | Searchable |

---

This is a strong record environment for the late 1700s — Quakers were meticulous record-keepers and their meetings predate civil registration by over a century. The main challenge is **access**: the richest records are at Swarthmore and Haverford or on unindexed microfilm, so knowing the specific monthly meeting your family attended is essential before you can work efficiently. If you know a county, I can help identify the likely monthly meeting or plan searches against specific Hinshaw volumes or FamilySearch microfilm.

# Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania
## Locality Research Guide — Late 1800s Steel Industry (c. 1870–1900)

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Pittsburgh is the county seat of **Allegheny County**, Pennsylvania, formed in 1788 from parts of Washington and Westmoreland Counties. One critical quirk: a separate **City of Allegheny** (directly north across the Allegheny River) existed as its own municipality until it was annexed by Pittsburgh in 1907. Families living there before 1907 generated records filed under "Allegheny City," not "Pittsburgh" — always search both.

Pennsylvania did **not** require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until **1906** (state level). However, **Allegheny County kept its own local birth and death registers beginning around 1870**, making it somewhat better served than most Pennsylvania counties for this era. Marriage licenses were recorded at the county courthouse throughout the colonial period onward. *(Source: [Pennsylvania Vital Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records))*

---

### ⚙️ Industrial & Occupational Records — Primary Focus

These are the records most directly tied to the steel industry:

| Source | What It Shows | Where Held | Digitization |
|--------|--------------|-----------|--------------|
| **Company employment records** | Hire dates, job classifications, sometimes birthplace and family data | Heinz History Center; Rivers of Steel archives | 🔴 Physical — fragmentary survival |
| **Union membership lists** | Membership dates, dues, sometimes addresses | Heinz History Center | 🔴 Physical |
| **City directories** | Annual name, occupation, and address listings | Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh; Ancestry.com | ⚠️ Partially digitized on Ancestry; physical from 1810s at Carnegie Library |
| **PA State Factory Inspector Reports** | Annual reports listing major employers, workforce counts, sometimes workforce nationality | Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | 🔴 Physical |
| **Federal census occupation columns** | Occupation listed in every census; 1880 Manufacturers/Industry Schedules add establishment-level detail | FamilySearch / Ancestry | ✅ Fully indexed |
| **Newspaper accounts** | Strike coverage, mill accidents, worker obituaries | Carnegie Library; Newspapers.com | ⚠️ Partially digitized |

**Company employment records are fragmentary.** Carnegie Steel and other major firms did not systematically preserve worker-level records. The Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel archives hold what survives, but gaps are large. Contact both repositories before visiting to check specific firms or date ranges. *(Source: [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records))*

**Key repositories for industrial research:**
- **Senator John Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) — premier repository for Pittsburgh and western Pennsylvania industrial and immigration records; holds select Carnegie Steel and company records, labor union archives, and immigrant community collections.
- **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area** — archives and oral history collections focused specifically on the steel industry; contact them before visiting.
- **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh (Pennsylvania Department)** — city directories from the 1810s, Pittsburgh newspapers, and regional maps.

---

### Vital Records

**Allegheny County local death and birth registers (c. 1870–1906):** Kept at the county level before statewide registration. These are the primary civil source for the target period. Check the Allegheny County courthouse and the Heinz History Center. Digitization is limited — mostly physical or microfilm.

**Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906–1968** — FamilySearch collection [1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317): 4,218,763 fully indexed records with images. Starts just **after** the target period but covers workers who lived into the 1900s.

**Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950** — FamilySearch collection [1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957): 312,045 indexed records with images. Covers the full target period.

**Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950** — FamilySearch collection [1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317): 524,189 indexed records with images; overlaps the target period from 1885.

**Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900** — FamilySearch collection [1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909): 198,765 records; **index only, no images.**

**Birth records:** No statewide registration before 1906. For 1870–1900, rely on Allegheny County local registers, church baptismal records, and family Bibles.

---

### Census Records

Federal censuses within the target window: **1870, 1880, 1890, and 1900** — all fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

- **1880 census** is especially valuable — it includes **Manufacturers / Industry Schedules** listing each industrial establishment, its output, and workforce by name.
- **The 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed by fire in 1921.** Pennsylvania has no state census that substitutes for this gap. City directories (published annually) and tax assessment records are the best intercensal bridges.
- **1900 census** records years in the United States — critical for immigrant steel workers.

---

### Church Records

Immigrant mill workers concentrated in ethnic parishes. Church records are often the **best source for family data** where civil registration is sparse. *(Source: [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records))*

| Community | Likely Denomination | Note |
|-----------|-------------------|------|
| Polish | Roman Catholic | Registers often in Polish or Latin |
| Slovak | Roman Catholic / Lutheran | Registers in Slovak or Latin |
| Croatian | Roman Catholic | Ethnic Croatian parishes |
| Italian | Roman Catholic | Ethnic Italian parishes |
| Irish | Roman Catholic | English-language registers |
| German | Lutheran / Reformed / Catholic | German-language registers common through 1900 |

Many Allegheny County Catholic and Protestant church registers have been microfilmed by FamilySearch — mostly browse-only. **Non-English registers require reading the original language.**

---

### Naturalization Records

Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in **any court of record** — Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas, U.S. District Court, or Orphans' Court. Naturalization records are at the **Allegheny County courthouse** and at **NARA's Mid-Atlantic Region office in Philadelphia** (which holds federal court records). Many are partially indexed on Ancestry.com. *(Source: [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records))*

---

### Immigration & Passenger Records

The primary port of entry for Pittsburgh's Eastern European steel workers was **New York** (Castle Garden to 1890; Ellis Island from 1892) and sometimes **Baltimore**. Passenger lists are indexed on Ancestry.com and partially on FamilySearch. Combine these with naturalization declarations, which often name the port and ship.

---

### Probate & Land Records

**Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** — FamilySearch collection [1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196): 893,214 indexed records with images. The county Register of Wills held wills, inventories, guardianship files, and letters of administration.

Pennsylvania land and deed records are held at the **Allegheny County courthouse**. The **Pennsylvania State Land Office** (Harrisburg) holds warrant, survey, and patent records. Tax/assessment duplicates for Allegheny County may serve as census substitutes and locate workers across the county. *(Source: [Pennsylvania Land Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records))*

---

### Newspapers

Pittsburgh papers — *Pittsburgh Gazette*, *Pittsburgh Post*, *Pittsburgh Press*, *Pittsburgh Dispatch* — covered labor disputes, mill accidents, and community news extensively. Search **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) for partial digital coverage. The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds physical runs and microfilm. **Worker obituaries and accident reports are important substitutes for absent death records before 1906.**

---

### Military Records

Civil War veterans are well represented in the steel workforce of the 1870s–1880s. **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/) indexes service and pension records. Originals are at **NARA** (https://www.archives.gov/).

---

### Repository Summary

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|-----------|---------|--------|
| **Senator John Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) | Company records (fragmentary), union archives, immigrant community records, city directories | In-person; some finding aids online |
| **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area** | Steel industry archives, oral histories | Contact first; in-person |
| **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** | City directories (1810s–), Pittsburgh newspapers, local history | In-person; some digitized |
| **Allegheny County Courthouse** | Marriage licenses, deeds, probate, court naturalizations, local vital registers | In-person |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)** | Factory inspector reports, state military records | In-person; some on Ancestry |
| **NARA Mid-Atlantic Region (Philadelphia)** | Federal court naturalizations, passenger lists | In-person; many indexed online |
| **FamilySearch** | Probate, marriage, and death collections (see above) | Free online |
| **Ancestry.com** | Census, city directories, passenger lists | Subscription |

---

### Digitization Summary

| Record Class | Level |
|-------------|-------|
| Federal census 1870, 1880, 1900 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| PA Civil / County Marriages (1885–1900) | ✅ Indexed + images |
| PA Compiled Marriages (to 1900) | ⚠️ Index only — no images |
| PA Probate Records | ✅ Indexed + images |
| PA Death Certificates | ✅ Indexed + images — **starts 1906, after target period** |
| Allegheny Co. local death/birth registers (1870–1905) | ⚠️ Mostly physical or microfilm |
| Church registers | ⚠️ Partially microfilmed; mostly browse-only or physical |
| Company employment records | 🔴 Physical only — fragmentary survival |
| Union membership lists | 🔴 Physical only |
| City directories | ⚠️ Partially digitized on Ancestry; physical at Carnegie Library |
| Pittsburgh newspapers | ⚠️ Partially digitized on Newspapers.com; physical at Carnegie Library |
| Naturalization records (pre-1906) | ⚠️ Partially indexed on Ancestry; physical at NARA Philadelphia and county courthouse |

---

### Key Quirks to Remember

1. **"Allegheny City" ≠ "Pittsburgh"** before 1907 — the north-bank municipality was a separate city; its records are filed under that name, not Pittsburgh's.
2. **Pennsylvania statewide death certificates begin only in 1906.** For 1870–1905 deaths, go to Allegheny County local registers first, then church burials, cemetery records, and newspaper obituaries.
3. **Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any local court** — search Allegheny County Common Pleas, U.S. District Court (NARA Philadelphia), and Orphans' Court, not federal courts alone.
4. **The 1890 census is destroyed.** City directories (annual) and tax assessment records are the best substitutes for that decade.
5. **Company employment records are fragmentary** — the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel hold what survives, but worker-level records are far from complete for most firms.
6. **Non-English parish registers** — Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, and German sacramental registers require reading the original language or Latin; do not assume English content.

---

The strongest starting points for steel-industry families are the **1880 census + Manufacturers Schedules**, **Pittsburgh city directories** (annual occupation and address snapshots), **ethnic parish registers** (often the only birth and death evidence before 1906), and an **in-person visit to the Heinz History Center**, which is the single richest repository for this exact research population.

# Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — Locality Research Guide
## Families Affected by the Yellow Fever Epidemic of 1793

---

### Jurisdictional Context

**Philadelphia city** and **Philadelphia County** both date from 1682 and coexisted as separate jurisdictions in 1793. The city occupied a compact area within the county; courts and probate operated at the county level while churches cut across both. They did not consolidate until the **Act of Consolidation, 1854**. For 1793 research, check both city and county repositories — a single repository may not hold all relevant records.

In 1793 Philadelphia was the **national capital** and the largest city in the United States, with a population of roughly 50,000. The yellow fever epidemic ran **August through November 1793**, killing approximately **5,000 people** — about one-tenth of the population. Thousands more fled the city. The disruption was severe: burial registers were overwhelmed, families were scattered, and normal civic record-keeping faltered during the worst months.
*(Source: [Wikipedia — Yellow Fever Epidemic of 1793](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793))*

Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil vital registration in 1793** — statewide registration did not begin until 1906. There was equally no city- or county-level civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths at that time. **Church records are the primary substitute for vital events**, and the epidemic's own published lists are a direct name source.
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records))*

---

### Priority Sources for the 1793 Epidemic

These record types were named specifically for the 1793 epidemic in FamilySearch Wiki results:

#### 1. Mathew Carey's Published Account of the Dead
**Type:** Printed name list | **Access:** Historical Society of Pennsylvania; widely reprinted

Mathew Carey published *A Short Account of the Malignant Fever* in 1793 containing lists of the epidemic's victims. This is among the most direct name sources for identifying who died during the outbreak. Multiple editions were printed. Check the Historical Society of Pennsylvania for holdings.
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever Epidemic of 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793))*

#### 2. Minutes and Reports of the Committee Appointed by the Citizens
**Type:** Civic relief records | **Access:** Historical Society of Pennsylvania; Philadelphia City Archives

The citizens' committee organized relief during the epidemic. Its minutes and reports document relief workers, aid recipients, and community response, and may name individuals not captured in church or probate records.
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever Epidemic of 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793))*

#### 3. Bush Hill Hospital Records
**Type:** Institutional/hospital records | **Access:** Philadelphia City Archives; Historical Society of Pennsylvania

Bush Hill was the primary hospital used during the epidemic. Its records may document patients admitted and deaths during the outbreak.
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever Epidemic of 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793))*

#### 4. Accounts by Mayor Matthew Clarkson and Dr. Benjamin Rush
**Type:** Contemporary narrative records | **Access:** Historical Society of Pennsylvania; printed

Mayor Clarkson and physician Benjamin Rush left detailed written accounts of the epidemic. These do not function as indexes but provide context, and Clarkson's administrative records may include lists of the dead or assisted.
*(Source: [Wikipedia — Yellow Fever Epidemic of 1793](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793))*

---

### Church Burial Records (Primary Vital Records Substitute)

Because Pennsylvania had no civil registration in 1793, **church burial registers are the main record of death during the epidemic**. Philadelphia's denomination landscape was wide:

- **Christ Church** (Anglican/Episcopal) — among the oldest in Philadelphia; burial registers survive for this period
- **Gloria Dei (Old Swedes' Church)** — the oldest surviving church in Pennsylvania; registers cover this period

Other denominations — Presbyterian, Lutheran, German Reformed, Methodist, Baptist, Catholic, and Friends (Quaker) meetings — each maintained their own registers.

> ⚠️ **Warning:** Burial registers from August–November 1793 may be compressed or incomplete. Churches were overwhelmed; some entries record mass burials without full identifying detail.

The **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records. Many colonial and early national registers have been transcribed and published in print. Check the **FamilySearch Catalog** by individual congregation for microfilm or digital availability — coverage varies widely by denomination and congregation.
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records))*

---

### FamilySearch Collections Covering 1793

Three collections in the FamilySearch catalog overlap the target period. **No death certificate collection covers 1793** — Pennsylvania statewide death certificates begin only in 1906.

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | Access Level | Link |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, Probate Records | 1683–1994 | 893,214 | 446,607 | Partial images | [Collection 1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | 156,023 | Partial images | [Collection 1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | **0** | **Index only — no images** | [Collection 1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) |

**Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900** is an index with no linked images. Use it to locate names, then seek the original church register for full document details.

The **Pennsylvania, Probate Records** collection is particularly valuable for 1793: the epidemic generated large numbers of sudden deaths and estates, and many children were orphaned. Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, and guardianship orders filed in Philadelphia County Orphans' Court appear here.

---

### Census Records (Bracketing the Epidemic)

| Census | Year | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1790 U.S. Federal Census | 1790 | Lists heads of household in Philadelphia immediately before the epidemic. Establishes who was present. Available on Ancestry and FamilySearch. |
| 1800 U.S. Federal Census | 1800 | Shows who remained in, returned to, or relocated from Philadelphia after the epidemic. Comparing 1790 and 1800 entries can reveal family disruption. |

*(Federal mortality schedules, which record deaths in the year preceding the census, begin only with the 1850 census — none exist for 1793.)*
*(Source: external_links_search — Ancestry.com U.S. Federal Census Collection; FamilySearch Wiki generic guide)*

---

### Probate and Court Records

The epidemic created sudden, large volumes of probate work. Key record types:

- **Wills and letters of administration** — filed in Philadelphia County Orphans' Court when a person died with or without a will
- **Estate inventories** — accompany most administrations; document household contents and economic status
- **Guardianship orders** — court appointments to care for children whose parents died in the epidemic

**FamilySearch**: Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (Collection 1999196) covers this period, with 446,607 images.
**Physical access**: Philadelphia City Archives holds original Philadelphia County probate records.

---

### Newspapers

Philadelphia newspapers published during the epidemic contain death lists, estate sale notices, and accounts of the crisis.

- **Newspapers.com** — historical newspaper archive, searchable by name *(confirmed in external_links_search)*
- **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** — holds original Philadelphia newspaper runs from this period

---

### Military Records (Context for Male Ancestors)

For male ancestors of military age, Revolutionary War pension files and service records may provide biographical context. These are held at NARA and available through **Fold3** *(confirmed in external_links_search)*.

---

### Cemetery Records

**Find A Grave** *(confirmed in external_links_search)* holds transcriptions of Philadelphia-area cemetery records and may document burials from the epidemic period. Many Philadelphia churches maintained their own burial grounds, and records may appear in both Find A Grave and in the church's own burial register.

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What They Hold | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** (Philadelphia) | Mathew Carey's account; Committee records; Bush Hill records; church record transcriptions; newspapers; personal papers | In-person; some digital |
| **Philadelphia City Archives** (Philadelphia) | Committee records; city institutional records; probate/orphans' court originals; deed books | In-person |
| **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** | Indexes to Philadelphia church records; compiled genealogies | In-person; some online |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Probate records; civil and compiled marriage records; FamilySearch Catalog (microfilm for church registers) | Online + microfilm at Family History Centers |
| **Ancestry.com** | 1790 and 1800 federal census; newspaper archives | Online (subscription) |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery transcriptions | Online (free) |
| **Fold3.com** | Military service and pension records | Online (subscription) |
| **NARA** | Federal census originals; military records; pre-1906 naturalizations | In-person (Philadelphia field office) and online |

*(Repository list grounded in external_links_search results and wiki_search results.)*

---

### Research Quirks and Warnings

1. **No civil vital records exist for 1793.** Pennsylvania statewide vital registration began in 1906. There was no city- or county-level civil registration in 1793 either. Church burial registers and Mathew Carey's published lists are the primary substitutes for death records.

2. **City and county were separate jurisdictions in 1793.** Philadelphia city and Philadelphia County did not consolidate until 1854. Some records filed under the city, others under the county — search both.

3. **Epidemic disrupted normal record-keeping.** Burial registers from August–November 1793 may be compressed, missing, or hastily recorded. Absence from a register does not mean an ancestor was not buried there.

4. **Thousands fled Philadelphia.** Families who evacuated may have generated records in neighboring counties or across the Delaware River in New Jersey. If an ancestor disappears from Philadelphia records in late 1793, neighboring jurisdictions are worth checking.

5. **Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (Collection 1502909) is index-only.** No images are linked. Find the name in the index, then locate the original church register separately for a full record.

6. **The FamilySearch Philadelphia Genealogy Wiki page** (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy) is the most Philadelphia-specific guidance available — the tool returned its content via keyword search but the direct page read was redirected to a generic guide. Visit the wiki page directly for additional detail on specific congregations and repositories.

---

### Coverage Gaps

- **Volume-level browsable image sets** (non-indexed FamilySearch volumes) were not inventoried in this survey — check the FamilySearch Catalog directly for Philadelphia County to find browse-only collections not surfaced here.
- **FamilySearch external links** for Philadelphia did not resolve to Philadelphia-specific curated collections — the links returned are generic genealogy sites rather than collections targeting Philadelphia 1793 specifically.
- **Population data** for Philadelphia County in this period was not returned by the place population tool.

# Locality Guide: Chicago (Cook County), Illinois — Great Chicago Fire, 1871

## Jurisdictional Context

Cook County was established in 1831 from the public domain; Chicago (the county seat) was incorporated as a city in 1837. By 1870 the county's population exceeded 350,000.

**The fire and what it destroyed.** The Great Chicago Fire burned October 8–10, 1871, destroying approximately 3.3 square miles of the city and killing roughly 300 people. Most critically for genealogists, it destroyed the **Cook County Courthouse**, which housed the county's official record repository: deed books, birth and death registers, court files (including naturalizations), probate records, and tax rolls. ([Wikipedia — Great Chicago Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire))

**Bottom line:** Pre-1871 Cook County official records are largely gone. Federal records held in Washington survived. A robust set of substitute sources exists — and is essential.

---

## What Was Destroyed vs. What Survived

| Destroyed | Survived |
|---|---|
| County deed books | Federal census schedules (originals in Washington) |
| Probate records (wills, inventories, guardianships) | City directories (Newberry Library, 1840s onward) |
| Cook County court records, including pre-1871 naturalizations | Chicago Title & Trust insurance/title records (Chicago History Museum) |
| Early tax rolls | Church registers of parishes outside the burn zone |
| Many church registers in burned districts | Relief society records (Chicago Relief and Aid Society) |
| County vital registration records | Newspapers — relief lists, death and missing notices |
| | Illinois State Archives records (held in Springfield) |
| | All military/pension records (held at NARA, Washington) |
| | Passenger arrival lists (NARA) |

---

## Record Types, Access, and Repositories

### 1. Federal Census Records ★ Start Here
The **1870 federal census** is your most important pre-fire household record — it survived because the originals were held in Washington, DC. The 1860, 1850, 1880, and 1900 censuses also survive intact.

- **Access:** Indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry.com
- **Tip:** Run the 1870 census (last pre-fire snapshot of household) alongside the 1880 census (shows where the family went after the fire). Illinois state censuses of 1855 and 1865 may also capture pre-fire household data — check the Illinois State Archives.

---

### 2. Vital Records (Birth, Marriage, Death)
FamilySearch holds three **indexed** Cook County civil vital collections — all beginning in 1871, when the county began local registration:

| Collection | Records | FamilySearch ID | Dates |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cook County Birth Certificates | 1,450,000 | 2024189 | 1871–1940 |
| Cook County Death Records | 980,000 | 1913456 | 1871–1947 |
| Cook County Marriage Records | 620,000 | 1756321 | 1871–1920 |

- **Access:** Indexed + images (name-searchable on FamilySearch)
- **Critical gap:** Illinois **statewide** vital registration did not begin until 1916. Cook County-level registration began in 1871. For births, marriages, and deaths **before October 1871**, there are no surviving official county records — you must rely on church registers, newspaper notices, and family papers.
- **Held at:** Cook County Clerk's Office for certified copies; FamilySearch for digitized images.

---

### 3. Church Records
**FamilySearch collection:** *Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925* — **285,000 records** (collection ID 1803978). Multiple denominations. **Indexed + images.**

**Beyond FamilySearch:**
- **Catholic parishes:** The **Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives and Records Center** holds surviving Catholic parish registers. Many pre-fire registers were kept at individual parishes; some survived outside the burn zone. Contact: [archives.archchicago.org](https://archives.archchicago.org)
- **Protestant parishes:** Registers vary by congregation. The **Newberry Library** holds transcriptions and abstracts for several Chicago churches.
- **Quirk:** If a parish register starts abruptly in 1871 or 1872, the earlier volume was almost certainly destroyed. Note the gap and pivot to other evidence.

---

### 4. Reconstructed Land/Property Records (Burnt Record Act of 1872)
The Illinois legislature's **Burnt Record Act of 1872** required all Cook County property owners to re-file deeds. These reconstructed deeds — accompanied by witness affidavits establishing pre-fire ownership — are the primary substitute for destroyed deed books.

**FamilySearch volumes found:**

| Volume | Content | Images | Indexed | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 009982110 | Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies), 1865–1871 | 38 | **0%** | **Browse-only — no search, must page image by image** |
| 009982111 | Post-fire Property Re-recordings, 1871–1880 | 112 | **41%** | Partially indexed; remainder browse-only |

**Beyond FamilySearch:**
- **Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD)** at Northeastern Illinois University: holds Cook County post-1871 records and some reconstructed pre-fire materials. Primary repository for Burnt Record Act filings.
- **Chicago History Museum:** Holds the **Chicago Title and Trust Company** records — the insurance/title company that became the de facto custodian of Chicago's property history after the fire. This is a *critical* source for any pre-1871 property research and should not be overlooked.

---

### 5. Probate Records
Pre-1871 probate files were destroyed in the fire. Post-1871 records:
- **Cook County Circuit Court Archives** (Richard J. Daley Center, Chicago)
- **IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University** (older transferred records)
- **FamilySearch microfilm catalog:** Some post-fire probate records are filmed; search the catalog by place.
- **Access:** Physical/microfilm — no indexed FamilySearch collection found for Cook County probate in this period.

---

### 6. Court Records & Naturalizations
Pre-1871 Cook County court naturalizations were destroyed. Post-1871:
- **Cook County Circuit Court Archives** holds county-level naturalizations (1871–1906)
- **NARA Great Lakes Region** (230 S. Dearborn, Chicago): federal court naturalizations post-1906 and some earlier federal district court records
- **IRAD:** Some county-level naturalization records
- For immigrants: **passenger arrival lists** (held at NARA, Washington) were unaffected and are searchable indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

---

### 7. City Directories ★ Key Substitute Source
Chicago city directories survive from the **1840s onward** and are among the most valuable substitutes for destroyed records. They list residents by name, address, and occupation.

- **1871 pre-fire directory:** documents where families lived before the fire
- **1872 post-fire directory:** shows who remained, who relocated, sometimes notes "removed to [new address]"
- **Held at:** The **Newberry Library** (primary collection). Also at the Chicago History Museum. Digitized and indexed on **Ancestry.com**.
- **Access:** Indexed on Ancestry (subscription); in-person at Newberry.

---

### 8. Newspapers ★ Key Substitute Source
Chicago papers covered the fire in exceptional detail, printing **lists of the dead, missing, and homeless**, as well as relief distribution rolls and personal notices.

- **Chicago Tribune** and **Chicago Times** (October–November 1871 issues are the most valuable)
- Available on [**Newspapers.com**](https://www.newspapers.com/) (subscription) and ProQuest Historical Newspapers (often free via public library card)
- **Access:** Digitized; searchable by keyword.

---

### 9. Chicago Relief and Aid Society Records
The Chicago Relief and Aid Society managed disaster relief after the fire and maintained detailed records of families who received aid — including names, addresses, household composition, and often nationality/origin.

- **Held at:** **Chicago History Museum** (manuscript collections)
- **Access:** In-person; finding aids available online at [chicagohistory.org](https://www.chicagohistory.org)
- **Tip:** For immigrant families, these records sometimes captured country of origin and family structure in ways that substitute for destroyed vital records.

---

### 10. Military Records
All federal military records were held in Washington and are fully intact.

- **Civil War service records and pension files:** [Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/) and NARA (subscription / in-person); **Access: indexed + images**
- **Illinois Civil War muster rolls:** Illinois State Archives, Springfield
- **NARA Great Lakes Region**, Chicago: some state-level and federal military records
- **WWI draft registrations (1917–18):** FamilySearch and Ancestry — indexed + images

---

### 11. Cemetery Records
Several major Chicago cemeteries predate the fire and their records survived:
- **Rosehill Cemetery** (est. 1859), **Graceland Cemetery**, **Calvary Cemetery** (Catholic, est. 1859)
- [**FindAGrave.com**](https://www.findagrave.com/): free indexed transcriptions and grave photographs
- Individual cemetery offices hold original interment registers.

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Newberry Library**, Chicago | City directories 1840s+, maps, manuscripts, church transcriptions | In-person; some digitized |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Chicago Title & Trust insurance records; Relief & Aid Society records; photographs | In-person; finding aids online |
| **IRAD — Northeastern Illinois University** | Cook County post-1871 official records; some reconstructed pre-fire records | In-person; some FamilySearch microfilm |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago — Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers | Contact archives: archives.archchicago.org |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records 1871–present | In-person; certified copies by request |
| **Cook County Circuit Court Archives** | Post-1871 probate, court, naturalization records | In-person (Daley Center, Chicago) |
| **NARA Great Lakes Region**, Chicago | Federal court naturalizations; some federal military records | In-person or written request |
| **Illinois State Archives**, Springfield | State-level records — entirely unaffected by the fire | In-person; some records online |
| **FamilySearch** | Digitized post-fire Cook County vital, church, and property records | Free at FamilySearch.org |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal censuses, city directories, newspapers, military records | Subscription |

---

## Recommended Search Order for Fire-Affected Families

1. **1870 federal census** — last pre-fire household snapshot (indexed, FamilySearch / Ancestry)
2. **1880 federal census** — where the family settled after the fire
3. **Post-1871 vital records** on FamilySearch — all three collections are indexed
4. **Church records** — FamilySearch collection 1803978; Archdiocese archives for Catholics
5. **City directories 1871 & 1872** — Newberry Library / Ancestry; pre- and post-fire address
6. **Newspapers, Oct–Nov 1871** — relief lists, death and missing notices (Newspapers.com)
7. **Chicago Relief and Aid Society records** — Chicago History Museum; especially for immigrant families
8. **Chicago Title & Trust records** — Chicago History Museum; for any property question
9. **Reconstructed deeds (Burnt Record Act)** — IRAD; FamilySearch volume 009982111 (41% indexed) and 009982110 (browse-only)
10. **Passenger arrival records** — FamilySearch / Ancestry (unaffected by fire; critical for immigrant families)
11. **Military / pension files** — Fold3 / NARA (unaffected by fire)

---

## Critical Quirks to Know

- **Pre-1871 Cook County official records are largely gone.** Deeds, probate, court files, and vital records held at the courthouse did not survive. Do not expect to find them on FamilySearch or at the courthouse.
- **The 1870 federal census survived** because the originals were in Washington — it is your best pre-fire household record.
- **Illinois statewide vital registration began in 1916**, not 1871. The 1871 start date on FamilySearch vital collections reflects when Cook County began *local* registration, not a statewide requirement. Before 1871, church registers are your only official vital source.
- **The Chicago Title & Trust collection at the Chicago History Museum** is essential for any property research — it filled the gap left by destroyed deed books and became the de facto title record for the city.
- **Look for post-fire family movement in adjacent counties.** Many displaced families relocated to DuPage, Will, Lake, and Kane counties; search those jurisdictions' records for 1872–1875.
- **Relief lists and newspaper notices are primary sources**, not supplements, for identifying fire victims and their circumstances — treat them as you would a vital record.
- **Sources grounded in:** FamilySearch Wiki — [Cook County, Illinois Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire); Wikipedia — [Great Chicago Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire)

## 📍 Locality Guide: French Colonial Louisiana (1700s)

**Place:** Louisiana, United States (French colonial territory: *Colonie de la Louisiane*)
**Period surveyed:** 1700–1769
**Jurisdictional note:** French administration governed the entire 1700s up to 1762; Spanish formal administration began in 1769. The years 1762–1769 are a transitional gap with thin official recordkeeping.

---

### Jurisdictional Overview

Louisiana was claimed for France in 1682 and settled substantively after 1699. New Orleans was founded in 1718 and served as the colonial capital. The colony was governed by the **Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur)**, which served simultaneously as court of law, registry of contracts, and administrative body — making it the single most important civil record-generating institution of the period.

**Critical boundary event — 1762 split:** By the **Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762)**, France divided the colony:
- **West of the Mississippi** → ceded to Spain (Spanish Louisiana)
- **East of the Mississippi** → ceded to Britain (became British West Florida / part of present-day Mississippi and Alabama)

Spain did not take formal administrative control until **1769**, leaving 1762–1769 as a transitional period with sparse, mixed-authority recordkeeping. Which side of the Mississippi River your ancestor lived on determines which colonial administration's records apply after 1762. This cannot be resolved from place name alone — you must establish the specific location before 1762 records or after.

*(Source: Wikipedia, "French Louisiana," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Louisiana)*

---

### Record Types, Repositories & Access

#### 1. Catholic Parish Registers ⭐ Primary source
**What they contain:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials. The Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church under French colonial law. The *Code Noir* (1724 Louisiana edition) required the baptism of all enslaved persons, so registers may document enslaved individuals as well as free settlers.

**Coverage:** St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans has registers dating from **1720**. Other parishes (Natchitoches, Pointe Coupée, Attakapas, Opelousas) generated registers when missions or churches were established, generally from the 1730s–1750s.

**Language:** Latin (sacramental entries) and French (marginal notations, sponsors). Researchers must be able to read both.

**Repositories:**
- **FamilySearch — "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"** (Collection ID: 1612905, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905): Overlaps the target period from 1718 onward. This is the most accessible online entry point. Access level not confirmed as fully indexed — browse the collection to assess.
- **Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans** — physical originals and/or microfilm for many pre-1800 registers.
- **Diocese/Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** — may hold originals not yet microfilmed.

**Key gap:** No civil registration existed in French colonial Louisiana. Parish registers are the *only* source of vital events for this period. If a person was not Catholic or lived in a remote settlement without a resident priest, no baptism, marriage, or burial record may exist.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records (1699–1762)," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)*

---

#### 2. Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) Records ⭐ Primary source
**What they contain:** Land grant concessions, civil and criminal court proceedings, contracts (sales, leases, apprenticeships), estate inventories, and wills. For many colonists this is the only record that places them in the colony at a specific date with specific neighbors or kin.

**Coverage:** Records survive from approximately 1714 through the end of French administration (1762/1769), though earlier records are fragmentary.

**Language:** French throughout.

**Repository:**
- **Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, 400 Esplanade Ave., New Orleans** — the primary physical repository. Records have been **partially digitized**; confirm what is currently online versus browse-only before planning a visit.

**Online access:** FamilySearch has no indexed collection specifically for Superior Council records confirmed in tool results. Check the Louisiana Historical Center's online catalog directly for digitized batches.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records (1699–1762)," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)*

---

#### 3. Notarial Archives (New Orleans Notarial Archives)
**What they contain:** Contracts, wills, marriage contracts (*contrats de mariage*), property transactions, manumissions, and powers of attorney — recorded before a notary as required by French civil law. This is the oldest continuous notarial office in North America.

**Coverage:** Records begin from the **1730s** onward through the colonial and later periods.

**Language:** French (and Spanish after 1769).

**Repository:**
- **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** — public access is available. Check their website for hours and online indexes.
- Some early volumes have been microfilmed by FamilySearch.

**Note:** Marriage contracts (*contrats de mariage*) recorded here are distinct from the church marriage register entry — both may exist for the same couple and each contains different information (property settlements, family witnesses, dowry terms).

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)*

---

#### 4. French Colonial Census Rolls (*Recensements*)
**What they contain:** Periodic enumerations of settlers, including household heads, family members, servants, enslaved persons, and livestock — essentially snapshot censuses ordered by the colonial administration. They are not uniform in format or frequency.

**Coverage:** Several survive for the 1720s–1750s. Coverage is spotty for remote settlements.

**Language:** French.

**Repository:**
- **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France** — the main archive for French colonial administrative records, including census rolls and administrative correspondence. Some holdings are digitized and searchable at [anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr](https://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr).
- Microfilm copies of selected ANOM holdings may be at the Louisiana Historical Center or on FamilySearch microfilm (search the FamilySearch catalog by "Louisiana" to identify specific film numbers).

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records (1699–1762)," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)*

---

#### 5. Land Grant Concessions & the American State Papers
**What they contain:** French *concessions* (land grants) were later compiled and reviewed by the U.S. government after the Louisiana Purchase. The **American State Papers: Public Lands** series documents claims confirmed or denied, often naming the original French grantee and date of the original concession.

**Coverage:** Useful for confirming land ownership in the colonial period even if the original French record is lost.

**Repository:**
- **American State Papers: Public Lands** — digitized and free at [memory.loc.gov](https://memory.loc.gov) (Library of Congress).
- **Louisiana State Land Office (Baton Rouge)** — holds additional Spanish-era and U.S.-era surveys of French concessions.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)*

---

#### 6. Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984
**FamilySearch Collection ID:** 2078341 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)
Estate inventories, wills, and succession records. Coverage begins 1756, overlapping the last years of French colonial administration. These may derive from either Superior Council proceedings or early notarial archives. Search this collection for colonists present in the 1750s–1760s.

---

#### 7. Military & Troop Records
French colonial Louisiana maintained a garrison of *troupes de la marine* (colonial marines). Muster rolls and officer records are held primarily at **ANOM** in France. These can document soldiers who settled in the colony and formed families. FamilySearch does not appear to have an indexed collection for French colonial military records in Louisiana within this period.

---

#### 8. Records Relating to Enslaved Persons
The Code Noir required Catholic baptism of all enslaved individuals, so baptismal registers at St. Louis Cathedral and other parishes are the main genealogical source. Superior Council records and notarial archives document sales, manumissions, and inventories that named enslaved individuals. These records are in French and may use given names only (no surnames). FamilySearch collection 1612905 (Church Records, 1718–1925) is the online starting point.

---

### Access Summary Table

| Record Type | Earliest Coverage | Repository | Online Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Catholic parish registers | 1720 (New Orleans) | Louisiana Historical Center; FamilySearch | FamilySearch collection 1612905 (1718–1925); browse to assess indexing level |
| Superior Council records | ca. 1714 | Louisiana Historical Center | Partially digitized — confirm at repository |
| Notarial archives | 1730s | New Orleans Notarial Archives | Partially on FamilySearch microfilm; physical access available |
| Census rolls | 1720s–1750s | ANOM, Aix-en-Provence, France | Partial digitization at anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr |
| Land concessions | 1700s onward | Louisiana State Land Office; Library of Congress | American State Papers free at loc.gov |
| Probate records | 1756 | Louisiana Historical Center; FamilySearch | FamilySearch collection 2078341 (1756–1984) |
| Military (troop) records | 1700s | ANOM, France | ANOM catalog; limited FamilySearch coverage |

---

### Key Quirks & Research Warnings

1. **French only — no English records.** All records from this period are in French (and Latin for church records). A researcher who cannot read 18th-century French script will need a translator or paleographer.

2. **No civil registration.** Vital events exist *only* in Catholic parish registers. There is no birth certificate, marriage license, or death certificate equivalent for this period. If no church record survives, the event may be unrecoverable from Louisiana sources alone.

3. **The 1762 split changes everything after mid-century.** After the Treaty of Fontainebleau, a family living west of the Mississippi generated Spanish colonial records; a family east of the Mississippi generated British records. Do not assume records after 1762 are in the same repositories as pre-1762 records for the same family.

4. **New Orleans fires of 1788 and 1794** destroyed significant portions of the city, and some records were lost. Gaps in parish registers and notarial volumes after these dates should be expected; look for reconstruction copies made by authorities after each fire.

5. **Parish system, not counties.** Louisiana retained the French/Spanish civil *parish* system rather than adopting the Anglo-American county. Records are organized by civil parish (which largely correspond to historic Catholic parishes), not by county. Searching by modern county name will not work for this period.

6. **ANOM is the shadow archive.** Many administrative records that do not survive in Louisiana — including some that were sent to Paris — exist in France at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer. A Louisiana research strategy that ignores ANOM is incomplete.

7. **FamilySearch wiki pages for Louisiana did not resolve to Louisiana-specific content** during this survey (all four `wiki_place_page` sections returned a generic guide). For current Louisiana-specific FamilySearch Wiki guidance, visit [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy) directly.

---

### Where to Start

For most French colonial Louisiana families, the recommended sequence is:

1. **FamilySearch — Church Records 1718–1925** (collection 1612905): search by surname for baptism/marriage/burial entries.
2. **FamilySearch — Probate Records 1756–1984** (collection 2078341): useful for the 1750s–1760s to find estate inventories that list family members.
3. **ANOM online catalog** for census rolls and administrative correspondence if the family cannot be placed from Louisiana-held records.
4. **New Orleans Notarial Archives** (physical or microfilm) for marriage contracts and property transactions from the 1730s onward.
5. **American State Papers: Public Lands** (loc.gov) to confirm land concessions and document a family's presence in a specific area.

# Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns — Locality Research Guide
**Time Period:** Late 1800s (ca. 1860–1905)

---

## Jurisdictional Overview

Pennsylvania's coal mining region divides into two distinct zones, each with its own county structure and record repositories:

**Anthracite (Northeastern PA):**
- **Schuylkill County** (formed 1811) — Pottsville, Mahanoy City, Shenandoah, Tamaqua
- **Luzerne County** — Wilkes-Barre, Plymouth, Nanticoke
- **Lackawanna County** (formed **1878 from Luzerne**) — Scranton, Carbondale, Olyphant
- **Carbon County** (formed 1843) — Mauch Chunk (now Jim Thorpe), Lansford
- **Northumberland County** — Shamokin, Mount Carmel

**Bituminous (Western PA):**
- Allegheny, Westmoreland, Fayette, and Washington counties

⚠️ **Critical jurisdictional quirk:** Lackawanna County was carved from Luzerne County in 1878. Court records, deeds, naturalizations, and probate for the Scranton area before 1878 are held under **Luzerne County**, not Lackawanna. Always search Luzerne first for events predating 1878 in that area.
*(Source: Wikipedia, Coal Region article — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_Region)*

---

## Record Classes and Access

### 1. Vital Records — ⚠️ Major Gap for the Target Period

Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil registration** of births or deaths during most of the late 1800s. The state's death certificate series begins in **1906** — evidenced by FamilySearch's "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968" (collection [2255317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317), 4.2 million records with images). This collection is useful for subjects who lived into the early 1900s, but covers almost nothing in the target window.

For the late 1800s, **church registers are the primary substitute for vital records** (see Church Records below).

**Marriage records** do survive for part of this period:
| Collection | Date Range | Records | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) | 1885–1950 | 524,189 | Indexed + images |
| [Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | Indexed + images |
| [Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | **Index only, no images** |

Marriage records offer a partial bridge, but coverage of the 1860s–1880s is fragmentary. Check all three collections.

---

### 2. Church Records — ESSENTIAL for This Region

Ethnic parishes were the backbone of mining community life and the **primary recorders of baptisms, marriages, and burials** for the period. The FamilySearch Wiki identifies these denomination clusters as common in coal towns ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)):

- **Irish Catholic** — dominant in Schuylkill and Carbon counties
- **Welsh Congregational/Baptist** — strong in Luzerne/Lackawanna (Scranton, Wilkes-Barre)
- **Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, and Ukrainian Greek Catholic** — heavy concentration in Luzerne and Lackawanna from the 1880s onward
- **German Lutheran/Reformed** — present across all regions

Church registers frequently contain far more family detail than civil records for this period. Check:
- The denomination's diocesan or presbytery archives (Diocese of Scranton for Catholic; Diocese of Allentown for Schuylkill/Carbon)
- FamilySearch microfilm holdings
- Local parish archives (many still hold original registers)

---

### 3. Census Records

Federal census schedules are the most consistently searchable record class for the late 1800s. Occupational fields identify miners directly. Key enumerations:

| Year | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1870 | Full | Lists all household members with ages, birthplaces, occupations |
| 1880 | Full | Adds relationship to head of household |
| 1890 | Largely destroyed by fire | Almost entirely lost — a critical gap |
| 1900 | Full | Adds month/year of birth, years in U.S., naturalization status |

All available through FamilySearch and Ancestry (indexed, with images).

---

### 4. Mining-Specific Records — Unique to This Region

These are records that exist *because of the coal industry* and are not found in ordinary county genealogical surveys.

**Mine Inspector Reports (annual from 1870)**
Published each year, these reports list every fatal mine accident with the worker's **name, age, nationality, and cause of death**. Held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg). This is a critical source for tracing immigrant miners who may otherwise be invisible in civil records.
*(Source: [Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))*

**Mine Worker Employment Cards — Schuylkill County (1870–1900)**
- FamilySearch image group 002240015 | 410 images
- Access level: **✅ Indexed (95%) + full-text searchable** — the most accessible mining-specific record found

**Mine Accident Reports — Luzerne County (1870–1895)**
- FamilySearch image group 002240016 | 287 images
- Access level: **⚠️ Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be examined image by image

**Colliery Payroll Ledgers — Lackawanna County (1878–1900)**
- FamilySearch image group 002240017 | 199 images
- Access level: **⚠️ Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be examined image by image

**UMWA Union Records**
The United Mine Workers of America (founded 1890) kept membership rolls and grievance files. These survive fragmentarily and are not fully digitized. The FamilySearch Wiki notes they are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives and at local historical societies.
*(Source: [Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))*

---

### 5. Naturalization Records

Immigration to the coal region was massive and continuous through the late 1800s. Naturalization is one of the most important gateways to identifying birthplace, which in turn unlocks records in the home country.

- Before 1906, miners could naturalize in **any court of record** — county common pleas courts near the mines are the first place to look
- **Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906)** are at the **Pennsylvania State Archives**
- Luzerne and Lackawanna County naturalizations are at their respective county courthouses and (partially) on FamilySearch microfilm
- Pre-1906 naturalizations are **not consolidated in one index** — check each county court separately

*(Source: [Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))*

---

### 6. Immigration / Passenger Records

Most miners arrived through **Philadelphia** or **New York** (Ellis Island opened 1892; Castle Garden preceded it). Passenger lists are at NARA and indexed on:
- FamilySearch (free)
- Ancestry.com

Many immigrants from Poland, Lithuania, Slovakia, Ireland, Wales, and Italy arrived in waves tied to industrial demand — knowing approximate arrival decade helps target the right passenger list series.

---

### 7. Probate Records

FamilySearch holds a large Pennsylvania probate collection that covers the target period:

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) | 1683–1994 | 893,214 | Indexed + images |

Wills and inventories for miners in this period sometimes name family members in other states or countries, providing immigration clues.

---

### 8. Military Records

The Civil War (1861–1865) falls at the opening edge of the target window. Pennsylvania raised a large number of regiments. Veterans appearing in the 1870–1900 censuses can be traced through:
- Service records and pension files: NARA (also on Fold3 and Ancestry)
- PA State Archives: Pennsylvania adjutant general records

---

### 9. Land and Tax Records

Mining families in company towns often did **not own land** (company housing was common), so land records may be absent. However:
- Tax lists survive at county courthouses and some are microfilmed at FamilySearch
- Miners who did purchase lots in borough plats will appear in deed books at the county courthouse recorder of deeds

---

### 10. Newspapers

Local mining-town newspapers are a rich and underused source — they covered mine accidents, strikes, union meetings, immigrant community news, and obituaries. Key papers:
- *Miners' Journal* (Pottsville, Schuylkill County) — one of the longest-running
- *Scranton Tribune* / *Scranton Republican* (Lackawanna)
- Available on **Newspapers.com** and at the **Pennsylvania State Library** (Harrisburg)

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | Location | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** | Harrisburg, PA | Mine Inspector reports, naturalization records, state-level series |
| **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** | Pottsville, PA | Local mining records, newspapers, family files |
| **Anthracite Heritage Museum** | Scranton (Lackawanna Co.) | Mining community records, ethnic collections |
| **County Courthouses** | Pottsville / Wilkes-Barre / Scranton / Jim Thorpe | Deeds, wills, naturalizations, court records |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Online (free) | Indexed collections, digitized volumes, microfilm |
| **Ancestry.com** | Online (subscription) | Census, passenger lists, county marriages |
| **NARA** | Philadelphia regional / Washington DC | Passenger lists, Civil War records, federal court naturalizations |
| **Fold3** | Online (subscription) | Military service records, pension files |
| **Newspapers.com** | Online (subscription) | Historical newspapers including *Miners' Journal* |

---

## Quirks and Cautions

1. **No PA statewide birth or death registration before 1906.** Births and deaths in the late 1800s are recorded (if at all) only in church registers or home-country records.
2. **Lackawanna County before 1878 = Luzerne County.** Search Luzerne for all Scranton-area events before Lackawanna was created.
3. **Carbon County formed 1843 from Northampton and Monroe counties.** Events before 1843 in Carbon County territory fall under those parent counties.
4. **"Miner" covers multiple job grades.** Census occupational designations don't distinguish miners from laborers, haulage boys, or surface workers — company employment cards (when available) give more specifics.
5. **Ethnic parish registers may be in a non-English language.** Polish, Lithuanian, Ukrainian, and Slovak registers from this period are often in Latin or the parish's native language.
6. **The 1890 federal census is almost entirely destroyed.** Use 1880 and 1900 on either side; state or city directories can partially fill the gap.
7. **Company records are fragmented.** Mining company employment records do not survive systematically — what exists is at the Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies on a company-by-company basis.

---

## Research Strategy Summary

1. **Start with federal census** (1870, 1880, 1900) to place the family in a specific township and county and confirm occupation.
2. **Identify the ethnic/religious community** and target the corresponding parish — church registers replace civil vital records for this period.
3. **Check Mine Inspector reports** at the Pennsylvania State Archives for any fatal accident reference; these give nationality and age.
4. **Search FamilySearch digitized volumes** — the Schuylkill mine employment cards (indexed) are a strong starting point; the Luzerne accident reports and Lackawanna payroll ledgers require browsing.
5. **Pursue naturalization** in the county court near the mine — this is the key to linking back to the old country.
6. **Search passenger lists** using the birthplace and approximate arrival decade.
7. **Check local newspapers** (especially *Miners' Journal*) for obituaries, accident reports, and community notices.
