# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (Early Puritan Settlements, 1620–1700)

---

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Two overlapping colonial jurisdictions existed during this period — **Plymouth Colony** (established 1620, the Pilgrim settlement) and **Massachusetts Bay Colony** (chartered 1628, settled 1630 by Puritan migrants). They operated as entirely separate governments until 1691, when the **Province of Massachusetts Bay** absorbed both, along with Maine.
- **Administrative center:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown
- **Population during period:** No formal enumeration survives; population data tools returned no figures for this pre-census era. Estimates place the English colonial population of the region at roughly 2,000 in the 1630s, growing to ~55,000 by 1700.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fishing, fur trade, timber, and coastal commerce.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers; small numbers of Dutch, French Huguenot refugees, and African enslaved persons in Boston by the 1670s-1690s.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalism was the established church of both colonies. Small numbers of Quakers (persecuted and sometimes executed), Baptists, and Anglicans were also present.
- **Key historical events:** Mayflower landing (1620); founding of Boston (1630); Pequot War (1636–1638); King Philip's War (1675–1676) — the deadliest per-capita war in American history, devastating many interior towns and destroying numerous local records; Salem witch trials (1692).

---

## Boundary changes

- **Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony were entirely separate jurisdictions, 1620–1691.** Records must be searched in the appropriate colony. Plymouth Colony records (1620–1691) have been **published and indexed separately** and must not be confused with Massachusetts Bay Colony records. ([Massachusetts Genealogy, Colonial Vital Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **County formation in Massachusetts Bay:** Four original counties were established in 1643 — **Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk, and Suffolk**. Land and probate records created before 1643 were held at the colony level; after 1643 they are held at the county level.
- **County formation in Plymouth Colony:** Plymouth Colony established its own counties in 1685 — **Plymouth, Barnstable, and Bristol**.
- **1691 merger:** The Province of Massachusetts Bay charter united Plymouth Colony, Massachusetts Bay Colony, and Maine into a single royal province. Records created after 1691 are held under the Province/State framework.
- King Philip's War (1675–1676) destroyed or severely damaged the records of many interior towns. Treat any absence of records for towns like Northampton, Deerfield, or Brookfield during 1675–1680 as possible war loss rather than non-existence.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Level:** Town (not county, not statewide)
- **Start date:** The General Court of Massachusetts Bay ordered **town clerks** to record births, marriages, and deaths beginning in **1639** — this is a **town-level** mandate. **Statewide** civil registration did not begin until **1841**. ([Massachusetts Genealogy, Colonial Vital Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **What exists:** For 1620–1639, there are no mandated civil vital records; rely entirely on church records and published genealogies. From 1639–1700, town clerk records of births, marriages, and deaths exist for many (but not all) towns — compliance and survival vary widely.
- **Digitized access — indexed + images:** FamilySearch holds **Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890** (Collection ID: 2061550, covering 1620–1890) at [familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550). This is the primary online access point.
- **Published transcriptions:** The multi-volume **Tanner–Corbin series** ("Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850") abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns and is widely held in research libraries. ([Massachusetts Genealogy, Colonial Vital Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **Gaps:** Towns destroyed or damaged in King Philip's War (1675–1676) may have no surviving records for the 1670s–1680s. Plymouth Colony vital records before 1691 are in separate published volumes, not in the general Massachusetts series.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalism was the established (state) church and the dominant record-keeper for 1620–1700. Small Quaker meetings (particularly in Rhode Island border areas and Nantucket/Sandwich), and a handful of Baptist congregations also existed by the 1680s.
- **Record types:** Member admission lists, baptisms, marriages, burials, and **disciplinary actions** (excommunications, admonishments). Disciplinary records are especially valuable — they name family members and contain biographical detail not found elsewhere. ([Massachusetts Church Records, Congregational — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))
- **Digitized access — indexed + images:** FamilySearch holds **Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920** (Collection ID: 1921657, covering 1630–1920) at [familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657).
- **Published transcriptions:** Many early Congregational records have been published by the **Colonial Society of Massachusetts** and in local historical society volumes. ([Massachusetts Church Records, Congregational — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))
- **Physical holdings:** Original registers are held at the individual churches (some still surviving), the Massachusetts Archives, and NEHGS.
- **Language:** English throughout.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first Federal census was 1790 — entirely out of period for the 1600s.
- **State/colonial census:** No general colonial census of Massachusetts survives for this period.
- **Substitute enumerations:** Colony-level tax lists and militia musters serve as population substitutes. The **1643 Able-Bodied Men list** (a military census of Massachusetts Bay) survives and is published. Town-level **rateable lists** (tax assessments) were compiled periodically and survive for some towns.
- **The Great Migration Study Series** (New England Historic Genealogical Society, Boston) is the most comprehensive substitute — it documents every known settler who arrived in New England **1620–1643**, with full biographical sketches and source citations. This is the single most important finding aid for researchers of this period. ([Massachusetts Genealogy, Colonial Vital Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))

### Probate and court records
- **Level:** County (from 1643 onward); colony court (before 1643 and for Plymouth Colony)
- **Types:** Wills, inventories, administration bonds, guardianship orders, and dower rights. Intestate inventories (for those who died without a will) are especially rich for the 1600s, naming household goods and naming relatives.
- **Date range:** County probate courts begin **1635** (Suffolk County being the earliest). Plymouth Colony probate is published separately.
- **Digitized access — indexed + images:** FamilySearch holds **Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991** (Collection ID: 1678901) at [familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901).
- **Colony and General Court records:** Records of the Court of Assistants and the General Court of Massachusetts Bay (1628–1686) are published in multi-volume series and held at the **Massachusetts Archives**.
- **Plymouth Colony court records** (1620–1691) are published in the 12-volume *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth* (edited by Shurtleff & Pulsifer).
- **Physical:** County probate court offices and the Massachusetts Archives (Boston).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Massachusetts is a state-land, not federal-land, state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Colony/state land grants. Original town proprietor grants were made by the General Court; individual lots were then distributed by town proprietors. This creates **two tiers**: colony-level grants to proprietors (Massachusetts Archives), and town proprietor divisions to individuals (town records).
- **Types:** Colony grants, town proprietors' records, deeds, and mortgage records.
- **Date range:** County registries of deeds hold deed records from the **1630s** in remarkably complete runs. ([Massachusetts Church Records, Congregational — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))
- **Where held:** Each county's **Registry of Deeds** holds the original deed books; many early volumes have been microfilmed by FamilySearch. Town proprietors' records are typically held at the **town clerk's office** or the Massachusetts Archives.
- **Access:** Deed indexes are largely physical-only or microfilm for the 1600s; some counties have partial online indexes.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Pequot War (1636–1638), King Philip's War (1675–1676).
- **Record types:** Muster rolls, militia lists, and pension records (for King Philip's War veterans, pensions were later granted). The **1643 Able-Bodied Men list** functions as a proto-military census.
- **Where held:** The **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) holds the bulk of colonial militia and war-related records. Published indexes and transcriptions exist for King Philip's War participants.
- **Online:** Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) holds some digitized military records, though colonial-era Massachusetts coverage is sparse. The Massachusetts Archives catalog should be consulted for specific conflicts.

### Cemetery records
- **What survives:** Church burying grounds and town cemeteries date from the 1630s. Many colonial-era gravestones survive in Massachusetts, particularly in Boston (Granary Burying Ground, King's Chapel Burying Ground), Salem, Plymouth, and other early towns.
- **Online:** **FindAGrave** (https://www.findagrave.com) has substantial Massachusetts coverage, including many 1600s gravestones photographed by volunteers. Coverage is uneven for small rural burying grounds.
- **Physical records:** Sexton's records (burial registers) for the 1600s are rare and often lost; the gravestone inscription is frequently the only surviving death record.
- **Transcription projects:** The Daughters of the American Revolution and local historical societies have transcribed many early Massachusetts burying grounds; transcriptions are held at NEHGS and local libraries.

### Newspaper records
- **Coverage:** Essentially none for the period. The first American newspaper, *Publick Occurrences* (Boston, 1690), was shut down after one issue. The *Boston News-Letter*, the first continuously published American newspaper, began only in **1704**. There are no colonial newspapers for the early 1600s that would carry vital or biographical notices.
- **Substitute:** Published sermons, election sermons, and funeral elegies (many held at NEHGS and the American Antiquarian Society) occasionally name individuals and families.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston and Plymouth were the primary arrival ports for 1620–1700 Puritan migrants.
- **Record types:** Ship passenger lists for the period are fragmentary. The most authoritative compilation is **Filby's *Passenger and Immigration Lists Index*** and individual vessel accounts in primary sources. The **Great Migration Study Series** (NEHGS) incorporates known arrival data for 1620–1643 settlers.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colony poll taxes and property assessments, compiled by town.
- **Date range:** Fragmentary tax lists survive from the 1640s onward for Massachusetts Bay; Plymouth Colony tax lists also survive in published form.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary substitute for census records during this period and can confirm a man's presence in a town and relative economic standing.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston); published in local history volumes and in the *Records of the Governor and Company of Massachusetts Bay*.

| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery records and gravestone photos statewide | Free |
| **Fold3** | Some colonial military records (limited 1600s coverage) | Subscription |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | Federal records — no 1600s Massachusetts holdings; useful for post-1790 research | Free/in-person |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) | Colony records, General Court records, court of assistants, governor's correspondence, militia and war records — 1620s onward | In-person; some digitized catalog |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** (Boston) | Largest genealogy library in New England; Great Migration Study Series; manuscript collections; published genealogies; NEHG Register | In-person; some collections online via AmericanAncestors.org (subscription) |
| **American Antiquarian Society** (Worcester) | Largest collection of pre-1820 American printed materials; essential for colonial-era newspapers, sermons, almanacs | In-person by appointment |
| **County Registries of Deeds** | Deed books from 1630s — Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk, Suffolk counties | In-person; some volumes on FamilySearch microfilm |
| **County Probate Courts** | Original probate files from 1630s | In-person; partially digitized on FamilySearch |
| **Individual town clerk offices** | Original town vital records (though most have been abstracted in the Tanner–Corbin series) | In-person or mail |

---

## Records NOT online

- **Town proprietors' records** (recording original lot distributions within each town) — mostly physical-only at town clerk's offices or the Massachusetts Archives.
- **Early county deed books** (pre-1700) — partially on FamilySearch microfilm, but not name-indexed; require browsing by image.
- **Colony court records** (Court of Assistants, General Court) — published in print but not fully digitized or indexed online.
- **Plymouth Colony records** — published in the 12-volume *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth* (widely held in research libraries), but not comprehensively indexed online.

- **Colonial militia muster rolls** — held at the Massachusetts Archives; not comprehensively digitized.

## Known record losses

- **King Philip's War (1675–1676):** Many interior Massachusetts towns were burned or abandoned during this conflict, destroying local vital records, town meeting records, and proprietors' books. 10. **FamilySearch wiki place pages for Massachusetts did not return Massachusetts-specific content** through the tools used in this survey; consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy for the most current online-records guidance.

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (Early Puritan Settlements, 1620–1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Two overlapping colonial jurisdictions — Plymouth Colony (1620) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628/1630) — merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691.
- **Administrative center:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown
- **Population during period:** No formal enumeration survives for this era. Estimates place the English colonial population at ~2,000 in the 1630s, growing to ~55,000 by 1700.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fishing, fur trade, timber, coastal commerce.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers; small numbers of Dutch, French Huguenot refugees, and African enslaved persons in Boston by the 1670s–1690s.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalism (established church); small Quaker, Baptist, and Anglican communities by the 1680s.
- **Key historical events:** Mayflower landing (1620); founding of Boston (1630); Pequot War (1636–1638); King Philip's War (1675–1676); Salem witch trials (1692).

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony were entirely separate jurisdictions, 1620–1691. Records must be searched in the appropriate colony.
- Massachusetts Bay established four original counties in 1643: Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk, Suffolk. Land and probate before 1643 are at the colony level.
- Plymouth Colony established its own counties in 1685: Plymouth, Barnstable, Bristol.
- 1691: Province of Massachusetts Bay charter united both colonies and Maine.
- King Philip's War (1675–1676) destroyed records of many interior towns.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Level:** Town
- **Start date:** 1639 (town-level mandate by General Court); statewide registration began 1841.
- **Digitized:** FamilySearch — Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (ID: 2061550)
- **Published:** Tanner–Corbin series 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' — 200+ towns
- **Pre-1639:** No civil vital records; rely on church records.

### Church records
- **Denominations:** Congregationalism (established church); Quaker meetings from ~1650s; Baptist from ~1680s.
- **Record types:** Member lists, baptisms, marriages, burials, disciplinary actions.
- **Digitized:** FamilySearch — Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920 (ID: 1921657)
- **Published:** Colonial Society of Massachusetts series; local historical society volumes.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- Federal census begins 1790 — entirely out of period.
- No colonial census survives.
- **Substitutes:** 1643 Able-Bodied Men list; town rateable lists (tax assessments); Great Migration Study Series (NEHGS) for 1620–1643 settlers.

### Probate and court records
- **Level:** County (from 1643); colony court (before 1643 and Plymouth Colony)
- **Date range:** From 1635 (Suffolk County)
- **Digitized:** FamilySearch — Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991 (ID: 1678901)
- **Physical:** County probate courts; Massachusetts Archives (colony court records); Plymouth Colony records published in 12-vol. Records of the Colony of New Plymouth.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds; state-land state.
- **Two tiers:** Colony grants to town proprietors (Massachusetts Archives); proprietors' divisions to individuals (town clerk offices).
- **Date range:** County deeds from 1630s in complete runs.
- **Access:** Deed books at county Registries of Deeds; some volumes microfilmed by FamilySearch; mostly browse-only or physical for 1600s.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Pequot War (1636–1638); King Philip's War (1675–1676).
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston); published indexes for KPW participants.
- **Online:** Fold3 has limited 1600s coverage.

### Cemetery records
- Colonial-era burying grounds survive from 1630s (Granary, King's Chapel, Salem, Plymouth).
- FindAGrave (findagrave.com) has substantial but uneven Massachusetts coverage.
- Sexton records rare for 1600s; gravestone inscription often the only death record.

### Newspaper records
- Essentially none for this period. First continuous newspaper (Boston News-Letter) began 1704.
- **Substitute:** Published funeral elegies and sermons (held at NEHGS, American Antiquarian Society).

### Immigration/emigration records
- FamilySearch 'Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891' does NOT cover the 1600s.
- Use Filby's Passenger and Immigration Lists Index; Great Migration Study Series.
- English port records (departing vessels) at The National Archives, Kew, England.

### Tax records
- Colony poll taxes and property assessments from ~1640s.
- Primary census substitute for this period.
- Massachusetts Archives; published in Records of the Governor and Company of Massachusetts Bay.

### Online
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Town Vital Records 1620–1890; Church Records 1630–1920; Probate Records 1635–1991 | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Various MA collections (thinner for 1600s) | Subscription |
| AmericanAncestors.org (NEHGS) | Great Migration Study; NEHG Register | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives (Boston) | Colony records, General Court, court of assistants, militia/war records — 1620s onward | In-person |
| NEHGS (Boston) | Great Migration Study Series; manuscript collections; NEHG Register | In-person; some online |
| American Antiquarian Society (Worcester) | Pre-1820 printed materials; sermons; almanacs | Appointment |
| County Registries of Deeds | Deed books from 1630s | In-person / microfilm |
| County Probate Courts | Probate files from 1635 | In-person / FamilySearch |

## Records NOT online
- Town proprietors' records (original lot distributions) — physical at town clerk offices or Massachusetts Archives.
- Colony court records — published in print; not fully digitized.
- Plymouth Colony records — published (12 vols.); not comprehensively online.

8. The NEHG Register (AmericanAncestors.org) contains thousands of articles on early Massachusetts families.
9. For English origins, check East Anglia, Essex, and Lincolnshire parish records — most 1620–1640 settlers came from these regions.

# Locality Research Guide: Oklahoma Territory / Early State of Oklahoma, 1889–1910

## Jurisdictional Context

This period spans **two parallel and successive jurisdictions**, which directly determines where records were created and are now held:

| Period | Jurisdiction | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-April 22, 1889 | Indian Territory (federal) | "Unassigned Lands" held by U.S. government; no settler civil government |
| April 22, 1889 | Land Run opens | ~50,000 settlers race onto the Unassigned Lands in a single day |
| May 2, 1890 | **Oklahoma Territory** organized | Capital: Guthrie; territorial courts, county governments begin |
| 1890–1907 | Two jurisdictions coexist | Oklahoma Territory (settler area) + Indian Territory (Five Civilized Tribes, separate) |
| Nov. 16, 1907 | **State of Oklahoma** formed | Both territories merge at statehood |

> **Quirk — dual-jurisdiction split:** Before 1907, a family's records may be in *either* Oklahoma Territory *or* Indian Territory depending on exactly where they lived. The two had separate court systems and separate record-keeping. Do not assume a family in "Oklahoma" was in Oklahoma Territory — confirm which jurisdiction applied to their specific location.

> **Quirk — origins research:** The FamilySearch Wiki notes that Land Run settlers came predominantly from Kansas, Texas, and Missouri. If you hit a wall in early Oklahoma records, searching those departure-state records is often necessary to find the family before 1889.

---

## Record Classes: What Exists, Where It Is, How to Access It

### 1. Land Records ⭐ (Prime Source for This Period)

These are the single most important record class for Land Run-era research. Every homesteader had to file federal paperwork.

**What they contain:** Original application, proof of settlement (with witnesses who knew the family), and the final land patent. Rejected applications survive too and can name family members.

**Where held:**
- **National Archives, Washington D.C.** — Record Group 49 (General Land Office). Homestead case files.
- **Bureau of Land Management GLO website** — [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) — searchable land patents, free online.
- **FamilySearch** — *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907* (Collection 1541872): 234,567 records, 117,283 images. Covers both the territorial period and pre-run Indian Territory grants. → [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872)

> **Quirk:** The homestead proof-of-settlement document required two witnesses who could attest to the claimant's residency — these witnesses are often neighbors or relatives, making land files a valuable FAN-club (family, associates, neighbors) source.

---

### 2. Census Records

| Census | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **1890 Oklahoma Territory Special Census** | Survives (partial) | One of the very few surviving 1890 census records in the nation. Held at the Oklahoma Historical Society. Covers early settlers in the newly organized territory. |
| **1900 Federal Census** | Full Oklahoma Territory | Fully indexed and online. The primary census source for this period. |
| **1910 Federal Census** | State of Oklahoma | Fully indexed and online. First census after statehood. |
| 1890 Federal Census | **Destroyed** | The national 1890 census was largely lost to fire in 1921 — the Oklahoma Territory special census is the substitute. |

**FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* (Collection 1987432): 567,890 records, 283,945 images. Covers tribal census rolls for Indian Territory families — essential if your ancestor had Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw, or Seminole ties. → [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432)

> **Quirk — Dawes Rolls:** Families in Indian Territory were enumerated on the Dawes Rolls (1898–1914), the definitive enrollment of the Five Civilized Tribes. These are separate from federal census records and are held at NARA and the Oklahoma Historical Society. Even families with partial Native ancestry may appear.

---

### 3. Vital Records

**Birth and death registration** was not required statewide in Oklahoma Territory (1890–1907). Statewide civil registration began after 1907 and was not fully enforced until the 1910s–1920s.

For the 1889–1910 window, primary substitutes are:
- **Church records** (see below)
- **County death registers** (filed at the county level, coverage varies)
- **Cemetery records** and **obituaries**

**Marriage records** are the exception — county clerks recorded marriages from the territorial period forward.

**FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995* (Collection 2134789): 456,789 records, 913,578 persons, 228,394 images. Covers marriages filed at the county level from the first year of territorial organization. → [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789)

---

### 4. Church Records

Denominations established congregations in new towns immediately after the 1889 run, though records begin **sporadically from 1889** and coverage is uneven in the first decade. Methodist, Baptist, and Presbyterian records are the most common.

**FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965* (Collection 1654321): 123,456 records, 61,728 images. Includes mission and denominational registers. → [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321)

**Repositories also to check:**
- Denominational archives (e.g., Oklahoma United Methodist Archives, OBU for Baptist records)
- Oklahoma Historical Society

---

### 5. Territorial Court Records (1890–1907)

District court records from the territorial period include civil cases, criminal cases, **probate**, and **naturalization** filings.

**Where held:**
- **National Archives at Fort Worth** — primary repository for Oklahoma Territory federal court records
- **Oklahoma State Archives** (Oklahoma City) — territorial and early state court records

> **Quirk — naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in *any* court of record — district, county, or probate courts. After Sept. 27, 1906, USCIS (then Bureau of Immigration and Naturalization) standardized the process. Check multiple courts for the same person.

---

### 6. Tax Rolls

County-level tax rolls from the 1890s are cited in the FamilySearch Wiki as a key source for documenting early settlers before census and vital records were well established. These are typically held at:
- **Oklahoma State Archives**
- **County courthouses**
- **Oklahoma Historical Society**

---

### 7. Military Records

**Where held:**
- **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) — service records, pension files, and draft registrations. Useful for Spanish-American War (1898) veterans, many of whom were Oklahoma settlers.
- **National Archives** (NARA) — service records and pension files.

---

### 8. Newspapers

Oklahoma Territory newspapers began publishing almost immediately after the 1889 run. The *Oklahoma State Capital* (Guthrie) and *Oklahoma City Times* are among the earliest.

**Where held:**
- **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com)) — historical Oklahoma newspapers
- **Oklahoma Digital Newspaper Program** — free access via the Oklahoma Historical Society
- **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress) — free, covers some Oklahoma territorial papers

---

### 9. Cemetery Records

- **FindAGrave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) — crowdsourced cemetery records including many early Oklahoma graves
- **Oklahoma Historical Society** — cemetery transcription projects

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **National Archives at Fort Worth** | Territorial court records, federal land case files, Indian Territory records | In person; some digitized via NARA/Ancestry |
| **NARA Washington D.C.** | General Land Office files (RG 49), military records | In person; partial online via BLM GLO, Fold3 |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** (OKC) | 1890 territorial census, tax rolls, newspapers, church records | In person + online: [okhistory.org](https://www.okhistory.org) |
| **Oklahoma State Archives** (OKC) | Territorial and county court records, vital records post-1908 | In person |
| **FamilySearch** | 4 indexed collections covering land, marriage, Indian censuses, church records | Free online: [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) |
| **BLM GLO website** | Federal land patents searchable by name | Free: [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census (1900, 1910), additional records | Subscription |

---

## Coverage Gaps to Note

- **No FamilySearch wiki pages specific to Oklahoma** were returned by the place-specific wiki tools — all four sections returned generic content. For deeper strategy, consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly: search [familysearch.org/wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/) for "Oklahoma" to find state-specific articles.
- **The 1890 federal census is destroyed** for virtually all of the U.S. The Oklahoma Territory special census (held at the Oklahoma Historical Society) is the primary substitute for that year.
- **Vital registration was sparse 1889–1907.** Church records, county death registers, and newspapers are the main substitutes for births and deaths in this period.
- **Indian Territory records are a separate research track** — the Dawes Rolls, tribal censuses, and Indian Territory court records require different sources than Oklahoma Territory settler records. If your ancestor lived east of the territorial line, start there.

---

## Where to Start

1. **Search the BLM GLO site** ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) for a land patent — it's free, fast, and confirms the ancestor's presence and location.
2. **Pull the homestead case file** from NARA (RG 49) — it often contains family details and witness names you won't find elsewhere.
3. **Search FamilySearch Collection 2134789** (County Marriages) and **Collection 1541872** (Early Land Records) for the 1889–1907 window.
4. **Check the 1900 and 1910 federal censuses** on FamilySearch or Ancestry to pin the household.
5. **If Indian ancestry is possible**, search Collection 1987432 (Indian Censuses and Rolls) and the Dawes Rolls.
6. **Search departure-state records** (Kansas, Texas, Missouri most commonly) for the family before 1889.

## Locality Research Guide: Alabama Region, c. 1780–1820 (Pre-Statehood)

---

### Jurisdictional Overview

Around 1800, there was no "Alabama" yet. The territory that would become Alabama passed through several overlapping sovereignties, and understanding that layered history determines where records were created and where they survive today.

| Period | Jurisdiction | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1702–1763 | French Louisiana (Mobile as capital) | French colonial administration |
| 1763–1780 | British West Florida | British colonial rule |
| 1780–1813 | Spanish West Florida (Mobile district) | Spanish re-took Mobile in 1780 |
| 1798–1817 | **Mississippi Territory** | U.S. organized territory; present-day AL was its eastern half |
| 1817–1819 | **Alabama Territory** | Split off from Mississippi Territory |
| 1819– | State of Alabama | Achieved statehood December 14, 1819 |

**The critical research rule for c. 1800:** Records created in the present-day Alabama area before 1819 were generated under Mississippi Territory authority (or, for the Mobile area, under Spanish administration until 1813). FamilySearch and NARA catalog many of these under *Mississippi* or *Mississippi Territory*, not Alabama. You must search both filing jurisdictions or you will miss the records entirely.

The early settlement pattern also matters: in 1800, European-American population was thin and concentrated near Mobile Bay in the southwest and along the Tennessee River in the north (Huntsville area, settled ~1805+). The interior was Creek and Cherokee territory until after the Creek War of 1813–14, so records created in the interior before ~1815 are extremely sparse.

*(Sources: Wikipedia — Alabama, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama; Wikipedia — Mississippi Territory, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Territory; FamilySearch Wiki — Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)*

---

### Record Classes and Access

#### 1. Territorial Censuses — 🟡 Microfilm/Physical; likely not name-indexed online

The Mississippi Territory conducted its own population counts in **1801, 1805, 1808**, and **1810**, separate from federal enumeration. These are the single most important census substitutes for finding individuals in present-day Alabama around 1800. They enumerate settlers in what is now Alabama as part of the Mississippi Territory. **Primary repository: Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery.** Some have been published in printed transcriptions by genealogical societies.

FamilySearch has a **"Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890"** collection (id: 1927171, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927171) which covers the territorial period and has some name-indexing; confirm whether specific territorial enumeration years are included for the Alabama portion.

#### 2. Federal Census (1810) — 🟢 Indexed + Images Online

The **1810 federal census** is the first federal enumeration that reliably covered the present-day Alabama area (the 1800 census predates much of the settlement push into the interior). It was taken under Mississippi Territory authority and is available name-indexed with images on both FamilySearch and Ancestry.com. FamilySearch collection: **"Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890"** (id: 2016756, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756). Note that the 1820 census is the first taken after Alabama statehood.

#### 3. Land Records — 🟢 Federal Patents Searchable Online; 🟡 Territorial Deeds on Microfilm

This is a **federal land state**: the U.S. government owned and distributed the land. The first federal land office opened at **St. Stephens** (Washington County) in 1803. Federal land patents from this period — the original grants from the U.S. government to private individuals — are searchable and downloadable free at the **BLM General Land Office Records website** (https://glorecords.blm.gov). These are among the most accessible digitized records for this period.

County deed books (private land transfers after the first grant) would be at county courthouses or on microfilm at ADAH. FamilySearch's **"Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907"** (id: 1919694, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694) covers the territorial-era land records and is the collection to search for pre-statehood Alabama land under the Mississippi filing.

**Spanish and British colonial land grants** (pre-1798, Mobile area) are a separate trail — see Colonial Records below.

#### 4. Tax Lists — 🟡 Microfilm/Physical at ADAH

Territorial tax lists survive for some Mississippi Territory counties that included present-day Alabama, and are among the best substitutes for a missing census before 1810. They name heads of household and list taxable property. **Primary repository: ADAH.** Some years have been published in genealogical journals or transcribed by the Alabama Genealogical Society. Not currently visible in FamilySearch's digitized volume catalog for this period (volume search returned zero results for Alabama 1780–1820).

#### 5. Militia Rolls — 🟡 Microfilm/Physical; Some Published

Territorial militia rolls name men of military age and predate pension records. The **Creek War of 1813–14** generated both militia muster rolls and, later, bounty land warrants and pension files at NARA. Pre-Creek War territorial militia rolls are held primarily at ADAH and in the NARA Territorial Papers. Some have been published by genealogical societies.

#### 6. Territorial Court Records — 🟡 Microfilm; County-Level

The Mississippi Territory established county courts that handled deeds, probate, guardianship, and civil cases. For present-day Alabama, the early territorial counties were:
- **Washington County** (organized 1800, southwestern Alabama — the earliest)
- **Madison County** (organized 1808, northern Alabama / Huntsville area)
- **Baldwin County** (organized 1809)
- **Clarke County** (organized 1812)

These court records — deed books, probate minutes, orphan's court files — were created at the county level and are the primary civil record source for the territorial period. Most are on microfilm at ADAH; some may be at county courthouses. FamilySearch's **"Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920"** (id: 1855293, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293) covers the territorial period under the Mississippi filing.

**Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985** (id: 1537764, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764) and **Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950** (id: 1598408, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408) begin in 1809, just before statehood — these will catch the last decade of the territorial period for the early-organized counties.

#### 7. Church Records — 🟡 Partial Digitization; Scattered Repositories

Civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths did **not** exist in territorial Alabama. Church registers are often the only record of vital events.

- **Catholic (Mobile area, primary for pre-1800):** Mobile's Catholic registers go back to the French period. These are the most historically deep church records in Alabama. Held at the Archdiocese of Mobile and/or Mobile Municipal Archives; some on microfilm.
- **Baptist and Methodist circuits:** Protestant circuit-rider churches spread through the territory in the early 1800s but record-keeping was inconsistent in this period.
- FamilySearch's **"Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950"** (id: 1986396, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396) covers the early territorial era. The **"Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950"** (id: 2034891, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2034891) may include additional records filed under Mississippi from the territorial period.

#### 8. Colonial Records (Mobile District, pre-1813) — 🔴 Physical; Overseas Archives

For ancestors in the Mobile area before 1813, you are researching in Spanish, British, and French administrative records:

- **Spanish period (1780–1813):** Census returns, Catholic church registers, and land grants for the Mobile District. Primary repository: **Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain.** Copies are at the **Library of Congress** (per FamilySearch Wiki). The Mobile Municipal Archives also holds microfilm. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records
- **French period (1702–1763):** Records at the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer** (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France; microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives.
- **British period (1763–1780):** British colonial records at the UK National Archives (Kew) and in the Colonial Office series; some published transcriptions.

These are specialized tracks requiring French- or Spanish-language competency and/or correspondence with overseas archives. None are digitized in FamilySearch's catalog for the Alabama filing.

#### 9. NARA Territorial Papers — 🟡 Microfilm; Some Digitized

NARA holds the **Territorial Papers of the United States, Mississippi Territory** (and separately, Alabama Territory 1817–19). These include correspondence, petitions, census-related documents, and administrative records that name residents. Series M969 covers the Mississippi Territory. Some portions are on microfilm; portions are available through the National Archives catalog (catalog.archives.gov).

#### 10. Military Pensions and Bounty Land Warrants — 🟢 Indexed at Fold3/Ancestry; Physical at NARA

Service in territorial militia and the Creek War generated federal pension and bounty land warrant files at NARA. These are among the most genealogically rich records — a pension file can include a veteran's age, birthplace, marriage date, wife's name, and residence history. **Fold3.com** (https://www.fold3.com) and **Ancestry.com** have indexed pension records with images.

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What's There | Access |

| **Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH)**, Montgomery | Territorial censuses, tax lists, militia rolls, county records on microfilm | In-person + some digital; archives.alabama.gov |

| **BLM General Land Office** | Federal land patents 1803+ | glorecords.blm.gov — free, searchable |

---

### Research Quirks for This Period

1. **Search under Mississippi, not Alabama.** Records created in present-day Alabama before 1819 were filed under Mississippi Territory authority. FamilySearch collections, NARA series, and microfilm catalogs file them under *Mississippi*. Always search the Mississippi filing in addition to Alabama.
2. **No statewide vital registration** existed in territorial Alabama. Church registers and court records (marriage bonds, guardianship files) are the only sources for vital events.
3. **The Mobile area has a separate colonial track.** Spanish (1780–1813), French (1702–1763), and British (1763–1780) administration generated their own record series in their own languages, held in overseas archives. If your family was in the Mobile Bay area before 1813, you need the Spanish/French colonial record trail in addition to U.S. territorial records.
4. **Interior Alabama is nearly blank before ~1814.** The Creek and Cherokee nations controlled the interior, and Euro-American settlement there was minimal before the Creek War. If your family appears in Alabama records after 1815, look for them in the Carolinas, Virginia, Georgia, or Tennessee before that date — that is almost certainly where they came from.
5. **Washington County (est. 1800) is the earliest county.** If your ancestor was in southern Alabama c. 1800–1808, Washington County court records are the first county-level source.
6. **The 1800 federal census does not cover this area.** Mississippi Territory was organized in 1798 but the 1800 federal census did not enumerate present-day Alabama. The territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (at ADAH) are your substitute.
7. **Alabama is a federal (public domain) land state.** County deed books begin at the point of first private sale, but the chain of title starts with a federal patent. Always begin a land search at the BLM GLO, then work forward into county deed books.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860s–1890s)

## Jurisdiction overview

| | |
|---|---|
| **Counties covered** | Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland |
| **County seats** | Pottsville · Wilkes-Barre · Scranton · Jim Thorpe · Sunbury |
| **Parent jurisdiction** | Pennsylvania, United States |
| **Schuylkill Co. formed** | 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties *(confirmed by place_search_all)* |

**Population — Schuylkill County** *(regional growth proxy, from place_population):*
1860: 89,510 · 1870: 116,428 · 1880: 129,974 · 1900: 172,927

**Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated all five counties. Collieries employed men as loaders, breaker boys, mule drivers, and contract miners at piece-rate wages.

**Ethnic composition:** Heavy Irish Catholic immigration from the Great Famine (1845–1855) onward, joined by Welsh, English, and Germans in the mid-century, then Eastern European immigrants (Poles, Lithuanians, Ukrainians, Slovaks) from the 1880s.

**Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant for Irish immigrants); Welsh Methodist and Congregationalist; Lutheran; Reformed; Episcopal. Coal-region Catholic parishes were established en masse between 1840 and 1870.

**Key historical events:** Molly Maguires labor conflict and trials in Schuylkill County (1860s–1877); the Long Strike of 1875; Great Railroad Strike of 1877; repeated mine disasters throughout the period.

---

## Boundary changes

- **Schuylkill County** (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton): stable during the target period.
- ⚠️ **Lackawanna County**: carved from **Luzerne County in 1878** — the single most important boundary fact for this region. All civil, court, and land records for the Scranton and Carbondale areas *before 1878* are filed under **Luzerne County**, not Lackawanna.
- **Carbon County**: formed 1843 from Monroe and Northampton counties. Records before 1843 are in Monroe and Northampton counties.
- **Luzerne County**: formed 1786 from Northumberland County. After 1878, the Lackawanna territory separated.
- **Northumberland County**: one of Pennsylvania's original counties (1772); covers the southern anthracite field around Shamokin and Mount Carmel; stable during this period.

**FamilySearch place coverage note:** The place_search_all tool confirmed Schuylkill at county scope (`Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States`). Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland all resolved only to the Pennsylvania state level — their FamilySearch volume and collection searches return state-scope results.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Births:** Pennsylvania had no statewide birth registration during the 1860s–1890s. Catholic baptismal registers are the primary substitute.
- **Deaths:** Pennsylvania statewide death certificates begin in **1906** — outside the target period entirely. This is confirmed by FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968" (id: 2255317, 4,218,763 records, **indexed + images**). For 1860s–1890s deaths: Catholic parish burial register → newspaper obituary → probate records → widow/widower status in the next census.
- **Marriages (county-level throughout this period):**
  | Collection | Date range | Records | Status |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 (id: 1921317) | 1885–1950 | 524,189 | **Indexed + images** |
  | Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (id: 1571957) | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | **Indexed + images** |
  | Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (id: 1502909) | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | **Index only — no images** |
  | Schuylkill Co. Marriage Records (imageGroup 007936753) | 1870–1910 | 94 images | **Browse-only** |

### Church records
- **Denominations:** Roman Catholic (primary for Irish), Welsh Methodist, Congregationalist, Lutheran, Reformed, Episcopal
- **Critical diocesan split:** The Diocese of Scranton was established in 1868, dividing existing Catholic parishes. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))
  - Parishes **formed before 1868** → baptismal registers held by the **Diocese of Harrisburg**
  - Parishes **formed after 1868** → baptismal registers held by the **Diocese of Scranton**
  - Since most coal-region Catholic parishes were established *between 1840 and 1870*, you must check the founding date of each parish before contacting archives.
- **FamilySearch volume (Schuylkill):** Church Records 1842–1895 (imageGroup 007936751, 187 images) — **browse-only images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable; contains both English and German records.** German registers require reading ability in that language.
- **Where held:** Diocesan archives (Scranton and Harrisburg); FamilySearch microfilm; individual parish offices for unfilmed registers.

### Census records
- **Federal censuses available:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910 — all **indexed + images** (FamilySearch free; Ancestry subscription)
- ⚠️ **1890 census destroyed:** A 1921 fire in Washington, D.C. destroyed most 1890 schedules — no surviving schedules for any of the five coal counties. See *Known record losses* below for substitutes.
- From 1880 onward the census recorded relationship to head of household — critical for establishing family structure in immigrant households.
- Pennsylvania did not take a state census.

### Probate and court records
- **FamilySearch collections:**
  - Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (id: 1999196, 893,214 records) — **indexed + images**, covers target period
  - Schuylkill County Probate Records 1851–1930 (imageGroup 007936749, 412 images, 0% indexed) — **browse-only**; search the statewide indexed collection first, then browse this county volume for records not captured there
- **Where held:** County courthouse (Orphans' Court / Register of Wills in each county)
- Probate records are a high-value substitute for vital records — they establish family relationships when birth and death certificates don't exist.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state, not a federal public-land state)
- **FamilySearch volume (Schuylkill):** Deed Records 1815–1900 (imageGroup 007936752, 543 images, **22% name-indexed**) — **partially indexed + images**; ~78% must be browsed after exhausting the name index
- Coal-region leases and surface/mineral rights agreements are a distinctive local record type; held at the county Recorder of Deeds
- **Where held:** County Recorder of Deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) for warrants and surveys

### Naturalization records
- **High-value for Irish immigrants:** Declarations of intention and petitions often state county of origin in Ireland, year of emigration, and age — more specific than most other record types
- **Pre-1906 rule:** Naturalizations could be filed in *any* court of record — county courts of common pleas, federal courts, and orphans' courts all took papers. Search all courts for each county, not just one.
- **FamilySearch volumes:**
  | Volume | Date range | Images | Status |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Schuylkill Co. Naturalization (imageGroup 007936750) | 1849–1915 | 298 | **Browse-only, 0% indexed** |
  | State-level Naturalization (imageGroup 008120443) | 1790–1915 | 351 | **15% indexed** |
- **NARA Philadelphia:** Federal naturalization records post-1906

### Military records
- **Civil War (1861–1865):** The coal region contributed heavily to Pennsylvania volunteer regiments. The **48th Pennsylvania Infantry** (largely Schuylkill County miners) is the most prominent coal-region unit.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files (NARA, indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry); Civil War draft registrations 1863 (FamilySearch, indexed)
- **Pension files** are especially valuable — they contain affidavits from neighbors and widows and sometimes record Irish place of origin
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. / Philadelphia); Pennsylvania State Archives for adjutant general records

### Cemetery records
- Catholic cemeteries were established adjacent to coal-region parishes from the 1840s; older headstones sometimes give Irish townland or parish of origin
- **Online:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves cover many coal-region cemeteries but coverage is incomplete
- **Physical:** Sexton records held by individual parishes and cemetery offices — **not systematically online**

### Newspaper records
- **Key papers:** *Miners' Journal* (Pottsville, Schuylkill County — founded 1825, the definitive coal-region paper); *Scranton Republican*; *Wilkes-Barre Record*; Carbon County papers
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, mine accident reports naming miners by name and colliery, Molly Maguires trial coverage, legal notices
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Library (Harrisburg — microfilm); Newspapers.com (subscription); Chronicling America / Library of Congress (free, partial digitization)
- Mining accident reports in newspapers are a unique substitute source: they name miners by name and colliery when the man doesn't appear in other record types.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia (primary for many Irish immigrants); New York (Castle Garden 1855–1890; Ellis Island from 1892); Baltimore and Boston also used
- **Pre-1895 passenger manifests** record name, age, sex, and occupation. **Post-1895 manifests** add last residence in the old country and contact in the destination — the fuller detail is valuable for tracing the chain migration network
- **Note:** Examine the full manifest page when searching a family — passengers are listed consecutively by family unit; infants and children traveling with parents are included
- **NARA Philadelphia** holds Philadelphia arrival records; FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription) index most arrivals for this period

### Tax records
- **Pennsylvania triennial state assessments (from 1853):** State assessors enumerated coal-region residents every three years. Ledgers list the householder's name, real estate value, occupation, and — crucially — sometimes nativity. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))
- **Gap-year value:** Assessments for 1888–1889 and 1891–1892 bracket the destroyed 1890 federal census; the nativity field can confirm Irish origin and place a miner in a specific township during those gap years
- Ancestry external link for Schuylkill: "Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801" (collection 7667) — pre-target period, but may document earlier family members

### ⭐ Specialized coal-region indexes
These sources are unique to the anthracite field and do not appear in standard locality surveys:

- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898:** Names approximately **41,000 colliery workers** across the lower anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation. Entries include occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and **parish of origin** where stated. This is the most direct genealogical finding aid for immigrant miners whose names were indexed inconsistently in census records. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))
- **Mine-inspection and accident reports:** Organized by *colliery*, not by individual name. Use payroll indexes to identify the colliery your ancestor worked, then consult accident reports for that specific colliery. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this region | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | PA County Marriages 1885–1950; PA Civil Marriages 1677–1950; PA Compiled Marriages 1700–1900; PA Probate 1683–1994; PA Death Certificates 1906–1968; Schuylkill Co. volumes (Naturalization, Church, Probate, Deeds, Marriage — see above) | Free |
| Ancestry | Federal censuses 1860–1930; passenger lists; PA tax exoneration lists | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (LoC) | Digitized historic Pennsylvania newspapers; partial *Miners' Journal* holdings | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Broader coal-region newspaper digitization | Subscription |
| FamilySearch Wiki | [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) — specialized coal-region index descriptions | Free reference |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill Co. Courthouse, Pottsville | Deeds, probate, naturalization, court records | In-person / mail |
| Luzerne Co. Courthouse, Wilkes-Barre | **All records for modern Lackawanna Co. territory before 1878**; all Luzerne records throughout | In-person / mail |
| Lackawanna Co. Courthouse, Scranton | Records from 1878 forward | In-person / mail |
| Carbon Co. Courthouse, Jim Thorpe | Records from 1843 forward; pre-1843 in Monroe and Northampton Cos. | In-person / mail |
| Northumberland Co. Courthouse, Sunbury | Records from 1772 forward | In-person / mail |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Colonial and state records, warrants, surveys | In-person / online request |
| Diocese of Scranton | Parish registers for parishes formed **post-1868** | Contact diocesan archives |
| Diocese of Harrisburg | Parish registers for parishes formed **pre-1868** | Contact diocesan archives |
| Lackawanna Co. Historical Society, Scranton | Local histories, coal company records | In-person |
| Schuylkill Co. Historical Society, Pottsville | Local histories, *Miners' Journal* files, family papers | In-person |
| Pennsylvania State Library, Harrisburg | Newspaper microfilm, published county histories | In-person / interlibrary loan |

---

## Records NOT online
- Most individual Catholic parish registers (not yet microfilmed or systematically digitized)
- Schuylkill County naturalization records are available as browse-only images only — 0% indexed
- County-specific volumes for Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland were not returned by the FamilySearch volume search (those counties resolve to state scope) — contact each county courthouse directly for record availability
- Mine company employment records outside the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index coverage area
- Sexton records for most Catholic cemeteries (held by individual parishes)

---

## Known record losses
- **1890 federal census:** Destroyed by fire in Washington, D.C., 1921. No schedules survive for any of the five coal counties. **Substitutes:** triennial state tax assessments (1888–1889 and 1891–1892 bracket the gap); city directories; church records; 1890 Veterans' Schedule (partial).
- **Coal company records:** The FamilySearch Wiki notes the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index was drawn from payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation — implying other company records were lost in that event. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))

---

## Research tips

1. **Lackawanna County before 1878 = Luzerne County.** Every record type — deeds, naturalizations, court papers, marriages — for the Scranton/Carbondale area before 1878 is in Luzerne County. Start there.

2. **Check the colliery payroll index before declaring a miner "not found."** The Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index (41,000 names, 1855–1898) catches immigrant miners whose names were mangled or missed in census indexing. It's the first specialized stop after the federal census. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))

3. **Identify the parish founding date before contacting diocesan archives.** The 1868 diocesan split means the wrong diocese gets a fruitless letter. Pre-1868 parishes → Diocese of Harrisburg; post-1868 → Diocese of Scranton. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))

4. **Death certificates don't exist for the target period.** Pennsylvania statewide registration began in 1906. Build your death evidence from burial registers, newspaper obituaries, and probate filings.

5. **Triennial tax assessments bridge the 1890 census gap.** The nativity column in years 1888–1889 and 1891–1892 can place an Irish miner in a specific township during the destroyed census year. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))

6. **Schuylkill County browse-only volumes require patience.** Naturalization (298 images), Church (187 images), Probate (412 images), and Marriage (94 images) volumes are all 0% indexed and must be browsed image by image. The Deed Records volume (543 images) is 22% indexed — search the name index first, then browse the remaining 78%.

7. **Church records volume contains German registers.** The Schuylkill Co. Church Records volume (1842–1895) mixes English and German records. German registers require reading ability in the language.

8. **Mine accident newspaper reports are a substitute source.** The *Miners' Journal* and other coal papers named miners killed or injured by name and colliery. If a miner doesn't surface in standard records, search the paper's accident coverage.

9. **For the FamilySearch Wiki Pennsylvania overview** (the wiki_place_page tool returned a generic fallback rather than PA-specific content), consult [Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Genealogy) directly.

That file includes a Sources section citing the exact wiki page and sections used.

Key takeaway from that page: **use payroll indexes, not just mine-inspection reports** — inspection reports are sorted by colliery, not by person, making them a secondary tool compared to the payroll-derived Lackawanna Valley index for individual name searches.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860s–1890s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Counties covered:** Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland
- **County seats:** Pottsville (Schuylkill), Wilkes-Barre (Luzerne), Scranton (Lackawanna), Jim Thorpe (Carbon), Sunbury (Northumberland)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Schuylkill County formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties (confirmed by place_search_all)
- **Population — Schuylkill County (proxy for regional growth):** 1860: 89,510 · 1870: 116,428 · 1880: 129,974 · 1900: 172,927
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated; collieries employed loaders, breaker boys, mule drivers, and contract miners
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish Catholic immigrant population from 1840s–1890s; also Welsh, English, German, and from the 1880s Eastern European immigrants (Poles, Lithuanians, Ukrainians, Slovaks)
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant for Irish immigrants), Welsh Methodist and Congregationalist, Lutheran, Reformed, Episcopal; coal-region Catholic parishes were established 1840–1870
- **Key events:** Great Famine Irish immigration 1845–1855; Molly Maguires labor conflict (Schuylkill County, 1860s–1870s); trials 1876–1877; Great Railroad Strike 1877; mine disasters throughout the period

## Boundary changes
- **Schuylkill County** (1811 from Berks and Northampton): stable during target period
- **Lackawanna County**: carved from Luzerne County in 1878 — the single most important boundary fact for this region. All records for the Scranton and Carbondale areas before 1878 are under Luzerne County.
- **Carbon County**: formed 1843 from Monroe and Northampton counties; records before 1843 are in Monroe and Northampton
- **Luzerne County**: formed 1786 from Northumberland County; after 1878 the Lackawanna territory became a separate county
- **Northumberland County**: one of the original Pennsylvania counties (1772); covers the southern anthracite field around Shamokin; stable in this period

**Note on FamilySearch coverage:** The place_search_all tool confirmed Schuylkill County at county scope (standardPlace: 'Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States'). The other four counties resolved only to the Pennsylvania state level, so their FamilySearch volume and collection searches return state-scope results.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Births:** No statewide birth registration in the 1860s–1890s. Catholic baptismal registers are the primary substitute.
- **Deaths:** Pennsylvania statewide death certificates begin in 1906 (FamilySearch collection 2255317, 4,218,763 records, indexed + images). For 1860s–1890s deaths: Catholic parish burial registers → newspaper obituaries → probate records.
- **Marriages (county level):**
  - Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 (collection 1921317, 524,189 records, indexed + images)
  - Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 records, indexed + images)
  - Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 records, index only — no images)
  - Schuylkill County marriage volume (imageGroup 007936753, 94 images, 1870–1910, 0% indexed) — **browse-only**
- **Where held:** County courthouse (Orphans' Court / Register of Wills)

### Church records
- **Denominations:** Roman Catholic (primary for Irish), Welsh Methodist, Congregationalist, Lutheran, Reformed, Episcopal
- **Catholic diocese split (1868):** Parishes formed before 1868 → **Diocese of Harrisburg**. Parishes formed after 1868 → **Diocese of Scranton**. Most coal-region Irish parishes were established 1840–1870, spanning this divide. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))
- **FamilySearch volume (Schuylkill):** Church Records 1842–1895 (imageGroup 007936751, 187 images) — **browse-only images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable; contains both English and German records** — German registers require reading ability in that language
- **Where held:** Diocese archives (Scranton and Harrisburg); FamilySearch microfilm; individual parish offices

### Census records
- **Federal censuses available:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910 — all indexed + images (FamilySearch free; Ancestry subscription)
- **1890 census:** Largely destroyed by fire 1921 — no schedules survive for any of the five coal counties
- **1880 onward:** Records relationship to head of household — critical for immigrant family structure
- **Pennsylvania did not take a state census**

### Probate and court records
- **FamilySearch collections:**
  - Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196, 893,214 records, indexed + images) — statewide, covers target period
  - Schuylkill County Probate Records 1851–1930 (imageGroup 007936749, 412 images, 0% indexed) — **browse-only**; check the indexed statewide collection first, then browse this volume
- **Where held:** County courthouse (Orphans' Court / Register of Wills)

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state)
- **FamilySearch volume (Schuylkill):** Deed Records 1815–1900 (imageGroup 007936752, 543 images, 22% indexed) — **partially indexed + images**; ~78% must be browsed
- **Coal leases and mineral rights** were a common document type in this region — held at county Recorder of Deeds
- **Where held:** County Recorder of Deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) for warrants and surveys

### Naturalization records
- **High-value for Irish immigrants:** Declarations of intention and petitions often state county of origin in Ireland, year of emigration, and age
- **Before 1906:** Could be filed in any court of record — county common pleas, federal courts, orphans' courts; search all courts for each county
- **FamilySearch volumes:**
  - Schuylkill County Naturalization Records 1849–1915 (imageGroup 007936750, 298 images, 0% indexed) — **browse-only, not full-text searchable**; must be browsed page by page
  - State-level Naturalization Records 1790–1915 (imageGroup 008120443, 351 images, 15% indexed) — partially indexed
- **NARA Philadelphia:** Federal naturalization records post-1906

### Military records
- **Civil War (1861–1865):** Coal region contributed heavily to Pennsylvania volunteer regiments; the 48th Pennsylvania Infantry (largely Schuylkill County miners) is the most prominent coal-region unit
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files (NARA, indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry); Civil War draft registrations 1863 (FamilySearch, indexed)
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington DC / Philadelphia); Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) for state adjutant general records

### Cemetery records
- **Catholic cemeteries** established adjacent to coal-region parishes from the 1840s; older headstones sometimes give Irish townland of origin
- **Online:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves cover many coal-region cemeteries but coverage is incomplete
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held by individual parishes and cemetery offices — not systematically online

### Newspaper records
- **Key papers:** Miners' Journal (Pottsville, Schuylkill County — founded 1825); Scranton Republican; Wilkes-Barre Record; Carbon County papers
- **Content:** Obituaries, marriage notices, mine accident reports (naming miners by name and colliery), Molly Maguires trial coverage, legal notices
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Library (Harrisburg — microfilm); Newspapers.com (subscription); Chronicling America / Library of Congress (free, partial digitization)

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia (primary for many Irish immigrants); New York (Castle Garden 1855–1890; Ellis Island from 1892); Baltimore and Boston also used
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry); declarations of intention and petitions (see Naturalization)
- **Pre-1895 manifests** record name, age, sex, and occupation; post-1895 manifests add last residence and contact in destination — the fuller detail is valuable for chain migration research
- **Note:** Examine the full manifest page for family groups — passengers are listed consecutively by family unit

### Tax records
- **Pennsylvania triennial state assessments (from 1853):** Enumerated coal-region residents every three years; ledgers list householder name, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))
- **Value for gap years:** Assessments in 1888–1889 and 1891–1892 bracket the destroyed 1890 census; the nativity field can help distinguish Irish immigrants
- **Ancestry link (Schuylkill):** Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801 (Ancestry collection 7667) — pre-target period but covers earlier family members

### Specialized coal-region indexes
- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898:** Names approximately 41,000 colliery workers across the lower anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation. Entries include occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and parish of origin where stated. The most direct finding aid for immigrant miners whose names were inconsistently indexed in census records. ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))
- **Mine-inspection and accident reports:** Organized by colliery, not by individual — identify the colliery from payroll indexes, then consult accident reports for that colliery ([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | PA County Marriages 1885–1950; PA Civil Marriages 1677–1950; PA Compiled Marriages 1700–1900; PA Probate 1683–1994; PA Death Certificates 1906–1968; Schuylkill Co. Naturalization 1849–1915 (browse-only); Schuylkill Co. Church 1842–1895 (browse-only); Schuylkill Co. Probate 1851–1930 (browse-only); Schuylkill Co. Deeds 1815–1900 (22% indexed); Schuylkill Co. Marriages 1870–1910 (browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | Federal censuses 1860–1930; passenger lists; PA tax exoneration lists | Subscription |
| Chronicling America | Digitized Pennsylvania newspapers including partial Miners' Journal | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Broader newspaper digitization including coal-region papers | Subscription |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill Co. Courthouse, Pottsville | Deeds, probate, naturalization, court records | In-person / mail |
| Luzerne Co. Courthouse, Wilkes-Barre | All records for Lackawanna territory before 1878; Luzerne records throughout | In-person / mail |
| Lackawanna Co. Courthouse, Scranton | Records from 1878 forward for Lackawanna territory | In-person / mail |
| Carbon Co. Courthouse, Jim Thorpe | Records from 1843 forward | In-person / mail |
| Northumberland Co. Courthouse, Sunbury | Records from 1772 forward | In-person / mail |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Colonial/state records, warrants, surveys | In-person / online request |
| Diocese of Scranton | Parish registers for parishes formed post-1868 | Contact diocesan archives |
| Diocese of Harrisburg | Parish registers for parishes formed pre-1868 | Contact diocesan archives |
| Lackawanna County Historical Society | Local histories, coal company records | In-person |
| Schuylkill County Historical Society, Pottsville | Local histories, Miners' Journal files, family papers | In-person |
| Pennsylvania State Library, Harrisburg | Newspaper microfilm, published county histories | In-person / interlibrary loan |

## Records NOT online
- Most individual Catholic parish registers (not yet microfilmed or systematically digitized)
- Schuylkill County naturalization records pre-1906 are available as browse-only images only — 0% indexed
- County-specific volumes for Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland were not returned by FamilySearch volume_search (those counties resolve to state scope) — contact each county courthouse directly for record availability
- Mine company employment records outside the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index coverage area

## Known record losses

([Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))
